AI infra startup Modal raises $750 mn at $15.7 bn valuation
Supriya Roy / Oct 14, 2026, 23:20 IST
Save
Comments
Share
Aa
+ Text Size
Small
Medium
Large Print
Modal co-founders (L-R) Erik Bernhardsson and Akshat Bubna
BENGALURU : AI infrastructure startup Modal Labs, co-founded by Delhi-raised computer scientist and Olympiad gold medallist Akshat Bubna, has raised $750 million that values the company at $15.7 billion. The fundraise comes as the five-year-old company crossed $1 billion in annualised revenue run rate, fuelled by growing demand for infrastructure that powers AI applications. The latest valuation is more than three times the $4.6 billion Modal was valued at in May this year, when it raised $355 million in a Series C round. The company’s valuation has risen more than 14-fold since September 2025, when it was worth $1.1 billion. Accel led the latest round, with Kleiner Perkins joining as an investor. Existing backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital and Bain Capital Ventures also participated, the company said on Wednesday. Modal said usage of its platform had tripled in the five months since its previous funding round, while the business had grown more than 15-fold year-on-year. Its annualised run rate, which reflects the pace of revenue extrapolated over a year rather than revenue earned in the preceding 12 months, has climbed from about $300 million in May to over $1 billion.
Founded in 2021 by Bubna and Swedish engineer Erik Bernhardsson, Modal provides computing infrastructure that allows companies to develop, run and scale AI applications without having to manage their own servers or computing hardware. Its platform now draws capacity from more than 20 cloud providers, allowing developers to access computing power as demand rises or falls. One of Modal’s fastest-growing businesses is Sandboxes, a product that allows AI agents to execute code in isolated environments. Launched in 2023, the product alone has reached a $300 million annualised run rate, the company said. Modal claims it has launched nearly three billion such environments to date and can support up to one million running simultaneously. The surge reflects growing adoption of AI coding agents, which need computing environments to execute programs, test results and carry out tasks. Modal said its infrastructure is used by companies including DoorDash, Cognition, Ramp and Runway, as well as robotics firms Physical Intelligence, Generalist AI and 1X. Modal is also expanding its products for AI model training and inference, the process of running trained models to generate outputs. Its latest launches include tools for training models across multiple machines and new capabilities for running AI applications. Bubna, who became the first Indian student to win gold at the International Olympiad in Informatics in 2014, previously told TOI that conventional cloud infrastructure was not designed for the demands of modern AI. In an interview last year, Bubna explained that Modal’s approach was to build its own software systems rather than depend on tools originally created for older computing applications. “One of the things programming competitions teach you is that most things are pretty solvable. You get used to solving harder problems,” he said at the time. The company has also expanded its workforce sharply. Modal had around 70 employees when Bubna spoke to TOI last year. It now employs more than 200 people across New York, San Francisco and Stockholm.

candidates.title: Weekly AI Funding: TypeSafe AI Hits $7.5B, Manus AI Raises $500M+ (Oct 7-Oct 12, 2026)
candidates.snippet: Weekly AI Funding: TypeSafe AI Hits $7.5B, Manus AI Raises $500M+ (Oct 7-Oct 12, 2026) AI Funding Tracker
candidates.text:
AI startups announced about $2.39 billion in primary funding across 14 rounds of $20 million or more between October 6 and October 12, 2026. TypeSafe AI’s $870 million Series A was the largest round, at about 36% of the total.
The largest disclosed AI acquisition was far smaller. Mexican financial group Kapital bought Woz Code, a US startup that makes a cost-cutting plugin for Claude Code, for $30 million.
North American companies raised $1.78 billion across nine rounds, or 74% of the total. Singapore-based Manus made up the whole Asia-Pacific share with more than $500 million, and four European startups raised $111 million.
Two deals need a plain-language note. Healthleap and Melius each announced a seed round and a Series A together, and the table shows the combined sum. No AI venture fund (money a VC firm raises from its own backers to invest later) closed above $20 million this week, and no employee share sale qualified.

candidates.snippet: AI infrastructure management software startup ASI hits $3B valuation after raising $325M in funding SiliconANGLE
candidates.text:
UPDATED 22:11 EDT / OCTOBER 20 2026
AI
AI infrastructure management software startup ASI hits $3B valuation after raising $325M in funding
by Mike Wheatley
An artificial intelligence startup called ASI Inc. , which builds complex models of air traffic and energy grids, said today it has scored $325 million in a Series C funding, bringing its valuation to a cool $3 billion.
The round was led by Spark Capital and joined by participants including Citadel Securities, Craft Ventures, Meritech Capital, Energy Impact Partners and Andreessen Horowitz.
The startup, which used to be known as Air Space Intelligence, is an AI company that develops frontier models designed to model physical reality and simulate future scenarios, so that its customers can plan and orchestrate how they operate critical infrastructure in real time.
It caters to companies in the aviation , defense and energy industries. For instance, it works with the Federal Aviation Administration and airlines such as United Airlines Inc. and Delta Air Lines Inc. to simulate and predict what’s happening in air space, so they can plan their flight operations. It gives pilots and air traffic controllers a way to plan ahead, reduce delays and increase flight safety and efficiency.
In addition, ASI works with the U.S. Army, U.S. Air Force and others, providing them with AI-driven command-and-control software that’s used to manage their daily operations. It also helps companies in the energy sector, including grid operators, enabling them to simulate their grid operations and plan for surges in demand.
ASI founder and Chief Executive Phillip Buckendorf (pictured) said he believes that future economic growth will be dependent on giving the people who run the country’s most critical infrastructure the ability to predict and forecast scenarios ahead of time, so they can avoid failures. “While the broader tech ecosystem spent hundreds of billions teaching AI to manipulate words and generate text, ASI is deeply focused on AI systems that can manage and control physical assets,” he stressed. “This capital ensures ASI scales as America’s engine: the automated nervous system keeping the country running.”
While hundreds of billions have been spent teaching AI to manipulate words and generate videos, ASI builds AI systems that can manage and control critical physical infrastructure – where there is zero margin for error.
Today we announced our $325M Series C to scale America’s… pic.twitter.com/l133h8H92E
— ASI (@AirSpaceIntel) October 20, 2026
The round follows a significant customer win for ASI. In June, it signed an $875 million multiyear agreement with the FAA to manage future air traffic across the U.S. with its AI platform. Impressively, it won the 12-year contract ahead of bigger and better known rivals such as Palantir Technologies Inc. and Thales SE, which both made aggressive bids, according to Bloomberg .
In air traffic scenarios, ASI’s system combines data from flight paths, real-time air traffic, weather and controller staffing to predict congestion and devise ways to get around problems and avoid delays. The FAA implemented the software at Dulles International Airport in Washington DC last month, and plans to expand it to all major U.S. airports in future.
The contract was a significant win for ASI, making the startup one of only four technology companies to land a federal contract of that size since 2000. Since then, ASI has secured another big contract with the U.S. Army. Earlier this month, it announced it had agreed a five-year deal worth $99 million to supply the military with AI software for its command-and-control program. Another big customer is National Grid USA Service Company Inc., which uses ASI’s software for planning purposes.
Going forward, ASI said the money from today’s round will help it expand further into the aviation, defense and energy sectors and also target new industries such as logistics. It’s also planning to grow its research and engineering teams with an eye to expanding the capabilities of its software.

Indian startups raise $2.9 Bn in Q3 2026 as EV, AI drive funding
Indian startups raised less than $3 billion in funding in Q3 2026, down from $3.5 billion in Q2 and $3.87 billion in Q1. The quarter saw fewer large funding rounds,
Shashank Pathak & Mukul Manchanda
01 Oct 2026
15:40

Follow Us
New Update
Indian startups raised less than $3 billion in funding in Q3 2026, down from $3.5 billion in Q2 and $3.87 billion in Q1. The quarter saw fewer large funding rounds, with Simple Energy leading the pack with a $182 million raise. The round also made Simple Energy the third-largest funded Indian electric two-wheeler OEM. Physical AI startup SiMa.ai, which has deep Indian roots and a major research and development centre in Bengaluru, raised another $150 million . Emergent, River Mobility, Navi, Slice and Pixxel also secured more than $100 million each during the quarter.
Despite the decline in overall funding, early-stage deals crossed the $1 billion mark in Q3. The quarter also saw six startup listings, including NSE, Rentomojo, Molbio, Milky Mist, Leap India and Purple Style Labs. Six startups shut down operations during the quarter.
[ Overview ]
According to data compiled by Entrackr, Indian startups raised approximately $2.9 billion in funding during the third quarter of 2026. This amount included 46 growth and late-stage deals totalling $1.89 billion, along with 194 early-stage deals worth $1.01 billion. Additionally, there were 26 undisclosed deals during the period.
[Q-o-Q and M-o-M trend]
Q3 2026 saw a modest recovery in startup funding compared to the same quarter last year. Total funding rose to $2.9 billion from $2.78 billion in Q3 2025, but remained below the $4 billion recorded in Q3 2024. September emerged as a strong month for funding, as startups raised more than $1 billion for the third time in 2026. February and June were the previous two months to cross the $1 billion mark, with each recording around $2 billion in funding. The September uptick helped Q3 close above the funding level recorded in the year-ago quarter.
[Top 15 growth-stage deals]
In Q3 2026, India’s top 15 growth and late-stage deals reflected strong investor interest in mobility, AI and fintech, along with bets across consumer and deeptech sectors. Simple Energy topped the list after raising $182 million in its Series C round, followed by physical AI startup SiMa.ai, which secured $150 million in Series C funding. AI startup Emergent raised $130 million , while electric two-wheeler maker River Mobility secured $120 million. Fintech firms Navi and Slice raised $100 million each, while electric mobility platform Yulu followed with $93 million. EV maker Ultraviolette raised $85 million, while AI startups Ema and Sarvam AI secured $77 million and $74 million, respectively. Wearable tech startup Ultrahuman raised $70 million, while The Pizza Bakery secured $56 million. Healthtech startup Nua raised $50 million, followed by Third Wave Coffee at $43 million and aerospace and defence company Raghu Vamsi Aerospace Group at $40 million.
[Top 15 early-stage deals]
Early-stage activity remained strong in Q3 2026, led by Pixxel’s $100 million Series A and Airbound’s $37 million Series A. Yuma Energy followed with $35 million, while Centricity and InRisk Labs raised $30 million and $27 million, respectively. Most of the top deals fell in the $15–25 million range, reflecting steady investor interest in early-stage companies.
Spacetech, fintech, deeptech and mobility featured prominently among the top deals. Data centre startup CtrlS raised $25 million, while foodtech firm Arboreal Bioinnovations secured $24 million . Business Nextgen Finance and Runable raised $21.7 million and $21 million, respectively. NeoGeo, Nexedge Capital and QNu Labs raised $20 million each, while Gravity, Piston and Plaza rounded out the list at $15 million each.
[Mergers and acquisitions]
The Indian startup ecosystem saw 33 merger and acquisition transactions in Q3 2026, covering sectors such as fintech, healthtech, AI, edtech, spacetech and e-commerce. Some of the notable deals included Samara Capital’s $120 million acquisition of stakes in Associated Road Carriers and Calyx Container Terminal, ITC’s $65 million acquisition of Yoga Bar and Udaan’s $52 million acquisition of Swiggy’s supply chain platform Lynk. Aurum PropTech agreed to acquire Housing.com’s parent in a $46.2 million share swap deal, while Ananta Capital acquired a majority stake in Phitku for $10.6 million. PhysicsWallah also acquired a controlling stake in Sarrthi IAS for $7.5 million. The quarter also saw strategic deals such as InsuranceDekho’s merger with RenewBuy, Adobe’s acquisition of AI startup Rilo and GalaxEye’s acquisition of spacecraft engineering company StarOps.
[City and segment-wise deals]
Bengaluru remained the leading startup hub in Q3 2026, accounting for 143 deals worth $2.1 billion, or 72.52% of total funding. Delhi NCR followed with 56 deals worth $296.76 million, while Mumbai recorded 31 deals worth $283.3 million. Pune and Hyderabad ranked next with 11 and seven deals, respectively.
AI led Q3 2026 funding activity with $635.3 million, followed by EV startups at $583 million. Fintech ranked third with $487.7 million, while e-commerce startups raised $222 million. Deeptech and healthtech followed with $123 million and $103 million, respectively.
[Series-wise deals]
Series C deals led Q3 2026 funding, with 11 rounds worth $887 million, accounting for 30.51% of total funding. Series A followed with 59 deals worth $689.17 million, while Series B deals raised $506.2 million across 19 rounds. Seed-stage startups recorded the highest deal count at 88, but raised $174.7 million during the quarter.

candidates.snippet: FuriosaAI raises $620 mn in Series D at $2.9 bn valuation to scale AI chips Beinsure

South Korea backs FuriosaAI through its National Growth Fund
FuriosaAI expands RNGD chip production to compete with Nvidia
FuriosaAI develops third-generation 2nm AI accelerator with Broadcom
International investors support FuriosaAI’s global expansion
South Korean AI semiconductor startup FuriosaAI has raised $620 mn in Series D financing, reaching a post-money valuation of $2.9 bn as it expands production of its RNGD inference accelerators and seeks to compete with Nvidia in the AI infrastructure market.
The Seoul-based company secured KRW370 bn ($280 mn) from South Korea’s state-backed National Growth Fund, making it the largest investor in the round. International investors contributed another $110 mn, according to the company.
FuriosaAI raised $620 mn in Series D financing at a $2.9 bn valuation, nearly quadrupling its valuation from July 2025.
South Korea’s National Growth Fund committed KRW370 bn ($280 mn), supporting FuriosaAI’s expansion in the AI inference chip market.
The company plans to produce 20,000 RNGD accelerators in 2026 and more than double production in 2027, while developing a third-generation 2nm chip with Broadcom.
The financing attracted demand from domestic and overseas investors, exceeding FuriosaAI’s initial fundraising target of KRW450 bn to KRW750 bn, Seoul Economic Daily reported.
The new valuation is nearly four times the $735 mn reported following FuriosaAI’s $125 mn Series C bridge financing in July 2025. Earlier that year, Bloomberg reported that the company had rejected an $800 mn acquisition offer from Meta Platforms, choosing to remain independent.
Founded in 2017, FuriosaAI develops processors designed specifically for artificial intelligence workloads. Its technology focuses on inference, the process of generating outputs from trained AI models, where electricity consumption and operating costs have become major considerations for data center operators.
The company is positioning its energy-efficient chip architecture as an alternative to Nvidia’s accelerators, which dominate the AI data center market.
“We see strong demand and opportunities as we are scaling our business globally,” chief executive June Paik told Bloomberg Television, citing customer engagement across the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East.
South Korea backs FuriosaAI through its National Growth Fund
South Korea’s Financial Services Commission said the National Growth Fund’s management committee approved KRW370 bn in direct investment from its Advanced Strategic Industry Fund on May 28.
The commission cited FuriosaAI’s independent technological competitiveness and said the financing was intended to help the company overcome funding constraints and compete internationally without interruptions caused by insufficient capital.
FuriosaAI is the second company selected under South Korea’s “K-Nvidia” initiative, following domestic AI semiconductor developer Rebellions, according to TheElec.
Rebellions received KRW300 bn in policy financing in March, including KRW250 bn from the National Growth Fund. The company also announced a $400 mn financing round that month, valuing it at approximately $2.34 bn, Reuters reported.
The National Growth Fund forms part of a five-year, KRW150 tn government initiative designed to direct public financing and private investment, including household savings, into strategic industries such as artificial intelligence and semiconductors.
By late May, the fund had approved 16 projects totaling KRW12.5 tn. Around KRW2 tn of its direct investment allocation had been designated for AI developers and semiconductor companies, including FuriosaAI, Rebellions and Upstage.
Several other government-linked financial institutions participated in FuriosaAI’s Series D.
The Export-Import Bank of Korea selected FuriosaAI for its first direct investment in a startup since its establishment, Seoul Economic Daily reported. Existing shareholder Korea Development Bank contributed an additional KRW30 bn.
Other returning investors included Naver, DSC Investment, Nextrans and Kakao Investment.
FuriosaAI expands RNGD chip production to compete with Nvidia
FuriosaAI began mass production of its second-generation RNGD accelerator, pronounced “renegade”, in January 2026.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) is manufacturing 20,000 RNGD accelerators this year, with FuriosaAI targeting production of more than 40,000 units in 2027.
The company said it had already secured the necessary memory supplies and semiconductor fabrication capacity to support the planned increase.
RNGD is designed to reduce energy-intensive data movement during AI inference, an approach FuriosaAI expects will improve efficiency compared with conventional accelerator architectures.
The processor is supplied as a 180-watt, air-cooled PCIe card. Eight accelerators can be combined in FuriosaAI’s NXT RNGD Server, which operates within a 3kW power envelope.
According to the company, the server can operate within existing enterprise racks and power budgets without requiring additional cooling infrastructure.
FuriosaAI claims RNGD can serve twice as many users per kilowatt as Nvidia’s RTX PRO 6000, although the comparison is based on the company’s own reported performance figures.
Energy efficiency has become an important purchasing consideration as demand for AI inference increases. Data center operators are seeking alternatives capable of processing growing workloads without proportionate increases in electricity consumption.
FuriosaAI has already secured several commercial deployments in South Korea.
Samsung SDS has introduced an NPU-as-a-Service offering powered by RNGD, allowing customers to access AI accelerator capacity through its infrastructure.

candidates.text:
Next-Gen Technologies
2 min read
Nuvacore startup raises hundreds of millions at $2.5 billion valuation for new data center processor
Nuvacore, a six-month-old startup, is raising significant funds for its central processor development aimed at data centers. The company plans to optimize chip design for common data center and AI computations, avoiding traditional architecture limitations. Founded by former Apple executive Gerard Williams, Nuvacore has already secured previous funding led by Sequoia Capital. Investor interest in semiconductor startups has increased significantly in recent months, surpassing previous funding totals.

Six-month-old microchip startup Nuvacore , which does not yet have a product, is raising hundreds of millions of dollars at a roughly $2.5 billion valuation to develop a new central processor designed for data centers , according to two people familiar with the fundraising.
Nuvacore is seeking to raise the funds as the appetite for central processors has swollen due to the thirst for data-crunching capacity to power chatbots such as Anthropic's Claude. CPUs perform vital functions as traffic controllers for Nvidia's AI chips and run autonomous AI software known as agents.
The roughly $2.5 billion valuation has not been previously reported. The Information reported previously that Nuvacore was raising $200 million or more. The funding round has not closed, and the people cautioned that the valuation and size of the capital raise could change.
Advt
Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, which use x86 technology, have long dominated the data center CPU market. Companies designing chips based on Arm's technology - found inside Amazon and Microsoft custom CPUs - have also attempted to make inroads in the data center market.
Nuvacore has not yet developed a product. Last month, it described an unconventional design strategy: to build the core functionality of the chip before committing to an architecture such as the x86 used by Intel and AMD, or Arm, which is used in most mobile phones.
The design strategy will allow the company's engineers to avoid the limitations and requirements of specific architectures and optimize a design for the type of computations that are most common in data centers and AI infrastructure, Nuvacore said.
Nuvacore declined to comment.
The San Jose, California-based startup was founded by renowned engineers Gerard Williams, John Bruno and Ram Srinivasan. Williams, a former Apple executive, sold a prior startup called Nuvia to Qualcomm for $1.4 billion in 2021.
Nuvacore earlier this year announced a seed funding round led by Sequoia Capital. It joins a series of young chip startups that have sought billion-dollar valuations before releasing a product as investor appetite for AI hardware companies has returned.
Over the past decade, Silicon Valley venture capital firms have taken much less interest in hardware than software because of hardware's longer development cycles, higher capital needs and the industry's cyclical demand.
Advt
Investors put about $10.7 billion into semiconductor startups in the first five months of 2026, already outpacing the $12.2 billion raised globally in all of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.
Earlier this year, Intel said it could not manufacture enough chips to meet demand, and was able to sell products it had previously determined were too faulty for sale. AMD also described swelling CPU sales in a recent results conference call with analysts.
Shares in both companies have risen more than 180% this year.
Nvidia launched a CPU called Vera this year. CEO Jensen Huang has said the company expects to sell $20 billion worth of its Vera CPU in this fiscal year, which ends in January.

candidates.title: Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation
candidates.snippet: Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the company announced it had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation.
The round comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled.
Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company.
Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT.
Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-old student-run startup accelerator that has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wrote Sequoia partner David Cahn , a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it.
The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.)
The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.”
The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” Asher Spector told TechCrunch shortly after the startup launched.
They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality.

SAN FRANCISCO , Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Blacksmith , the infrastructure platform for building and testing code, today announced a $66M Series C led by Sequoia Capital at a $1 billion valuation, with participation from Premji Invest and existing investors Peak XV Partners, GV and Y Combinator. The round brings Blacksmith's total funding to $125 million and will enable the company to grow its team and expand its compute footprint.
Continue Reading
Blacksmith announces its Series C, led by Sequoia Capital at a $1 billion valuation.
For years, writing code was the slow part of shipping software. With AI coding agents now producing a large and growing share of the world's code, the burden has changed from writing code to validating it. Every change still has to be built and tested before it can be merged, a step known as continuous integration, or CI.
Most companies run CI on general-purpose cloud infrastructure that was never designed for it. As developers push more code, teams hit longer waits for compute, slower builds on older-generation CPUs, and a constant fight between over- and under-provisioning. Anthropic reported last month that its own CI volume grew 25x in six months as Claude took over most of its code output.
"Since Claude Code took off in March, almost every conversation we've had with a large engineering team has started the same way. Developers who used to push three or four pull requests a day are now pushing orders of magnitude more and their CI infrastructure can't keep up. We're grateful to our customers who are trusting us to solve this bottleneck, and excited to partner with Sequoia to solve it at scale," said Aditya "JP" Jayaprakash, co-founder and CEO of Blacksmith.
CI is the most variable workload a company runs: a single customer's demand regularly jumps from zero to tens of thousands of CPUs and back again. Blacksmith has designed every part of its infrastructure stack to absorb those spikes as a matter of routine. Customers switch with a one-line change to their workflow file and never provision, scale or maintain their CI infrastructure again. Developers using Blacksmith see their CI jobs complete twice as fast and at 60% lower cost on average, with zero operational overhead. Since January, the number of CI jobs running on Blacksmith each week has grown from 5 million to more than 90 million, and annual recurring revenue has grown 17x.
"JP and team understood early that as AI agents wrote more code, the infrastructure to build and test it would need to change," said Isaiah Boone, Partner at Sequoia Capital. "What stood out to us was their deep systems expertise and speed of execution. That has translated into a product that helps their customers test and ship their software faster. We believe that foundation gives Blacksmith room to build much more as the demands of software development change."
Blacksmith was founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, who met as undergraduates at the University of Waterloo. Shah and Maru were early engineers at Cockroach Labs, and Jayaprakash was an engineer at Faire. All three are developers who have run spiky, large-scale infrastructure before, and they built Blacksmith on the bet that testing code, not writing it, would become the constraint on shipping software.
More than 10,000 companies, including Ashby, Granola, Handshake and LangChain, now run their CI on Blacksmith. The company manages nearly 10 MW of compute across data centers in the United States and Europe and is on track to grow that footprint at least 5x in 2027.
"Blacksmith has significantly reduced the burden of managing our CI runners while cutting our runner costs by roughly 40%, and that doesn't even account for the engineering time we've saved," said Joaquin Borggio, Infrastructure Engineer at LangChain.
To learn more or move your CI to Blacksmith, visit blacksmith.sh . Blacksmith is hiring engineers in New York and San Francisco at blacksmith.sh/careers . Follow Blacksmith on LinkedIn and X .
About Blacksmith
Blacksmith is the infrastructure platform for building and testing code. Companies bring Blacksmith their builds and tests, and Blacksmith runs them twice as fast and at 60% lower cost on average, on infrastructure purpose-built for CI workloads. More than 10,000 companies, including Ashby, Granola, Handshake and LangChain, run their CI on Blacksmith. The company was founded in 2024 by Aditya (JP) Jayaprakash, Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru and is backed by Sequoia Capital, Premji Invest, Peak XV Partners, GV and Y Combinator. For more information, visit blacksmith.sh .

candidates.text:
Funding
TypeSafe AI Raises $870M Series A at $7.5B Valuation to Ship More AI Models
Published
October 9, 2026
By
Evan Mercer, AI Startups & Venture Capital AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
TypeSafe AI announced on October 9, 2026 that it has raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz with participation from Sequoia Capital, existing investor DCVC, and angel investors. Andreessen Horowitz general partner Martin Casado is joining the company’s board.
Round Terms and Investors
Andreessen Horowitz confirmed it is leading the investment in a post dated October 9, 2026 and bylined by Jennifer Li, Sarah Wang, Martin Casado, Marc Andreessen, and Ben Horowitz. Li and Casado are general partners focused on the firm’s infrastructure investing, Wang is a general partner on its growth team, and Andreessen and Horowitz are the firm’s cofounders and general partners.
TypeSafe’s own announcement is a short post addressed to developers, businesses, and potential recruits; the company disclosed the dollar amount, the valuation, and Casado’s board seat in a footnote to that post.
The System One Model Behind the Round
TypeSafe released Jev in early access on September 15, 2026, after two years in stealth, and said it is bringing developers off its waitlist. In the launch post , founder Diogo Almeida described Jev as the first entry in a new model class the company calls System One, designed for rapid, structured decision-making inside software.
According to TypeSafe’s documentation , Jev takes typed questions and evaluates them against a supplied state, returning structured results without generating or parsing text. The results arrive as typed values with probability distributions, so code can branch, sort, and route on them directly. The company exposes three primitives: Choice picks one option out of a provided list; Score grades the state against a rubric; and Noul returns a 0–1 answer to whether a given statement is true. Choice and Score also return confidence values, and all three question types can be combined in one API call, where each is evaluated independently and concurrently against the same state.
Almeida wrote that TypeSafe built a new stack focused entirely on automation: a new model architecture, a parallel sampler, and a training method the company calls Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). He said Jev achieves similar intelligence to existing large language models on System One tasks while running two orders of magnitude faster, with end-to-end response times of 70 to 500 milliseconds, a range the post states can be 40 to 200 times faster than frontier models at comparable intelligence for System One–shaped queries. Because outputs are type-safe structured values defined in advance, Almeida wrote, the model never makes type errors and cannot hallucinate.
Published pricing is $0.042 per million input tokens, with output tokens free. The company states that the 193.6-times-faster and 444.6-times-cheaper figures on its homepage come from its workflow evaluations, and it cautions that those numbers are on the higher end of real-world gains. It also notes that the evaluation workflows were built by members of its model capabilities team and that some bias could exist.
Almeida wrote that at OpenAI he helped develop instruction-following methods for language models, work he said became the research behind ChatGPT. The System One name references Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow and its contrast between quick, intuitive System 1 thinking and slower, deliberate System 2 reasoning. Jev is named after William Stanley Jevons; the company said it expects machine intelligence to follow the path of coal, for which steam-engine efficiency gains led to increased demand.
Reported Adoption and Early Deployment
TypeSafe said in its announcement that a third of the Fortune 500 are using Jev and that it has already saved customers millions of dollars in production. The Andreessen Horowitz post states a different figure, saying 25% of Fortune 500 enterprises have integrated Jev. The firm described Jev as the fastest-growing model it has seen, stating that it reached 1 trillion tokens generated within three days of launch and that thousands of use cases surfaced during the first week, among them generative UI, interactive gaming, and data analysis. It characterized Jev as roughly 1/100 to 1/500 the cost of frontier models while being 100 times faster for classification tasks at comparable accuracy, passing model decisions straight into code as typed values rather than text that software must then parse.
In an October 7, 2026 case study , TypeSafe reported that Jack & Jill, a talent marketplace where AI agents match candidates with hiring teams, replaced Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite for 100% of calls in a key stage of its candidate-matching pipeline within 10 days of its first test. According to the case study, the change cut screening costs by 88%, from $0.755 to $0.092 per 1,000 candidates, and halved median screening time from 20.3 seconds to 10.3 seconds, while retaining 94.6% of candidates that hiring managers later asked to meet, compared with a 93.9% baseline; the study notes that this quality difference was not statistically significant. Ranking quality measured 0.933 for Jev versus 0.924 for Gemini on AUC. TypeSafe reported $265,000 in annual savings for Jack & Jill at current volume, with $500,000 projected over the next twelve months given expected growth, and said Jev usage has expanded to more than 15 workflows, including matched roles shown to candidates at sign-up and a profile check that fell from about 3.6 seconds to about 0.2 seconds.
Stated Plans
TypeSafe said it intends to take Jev’s capabilities further, ship additional machine-native models, provide infrastructure for building smart software, and add the enterprise features customers have requested. The announcement also encourages potent

candidates.title: Structured-Decision AI Maker TypeSafe Raises $870M Series A
candidates.snippet: Structured-Decision AI Maker TypeSafe Raises $870M Series A Wowtale
candidates.text:
As AI agents spread across the industry, investment is piling into an infrastructure layer that skips long, human-readable text responses and instead hands software a judgment it can consume directly. The promise of solving speed, cost and reliability at once is moving investors fast.
TypeSafe AI sits at the center of that shift. Last month the company came out of stealth with a $40 million seed round for its structured-decision model, Jev. Unlike a conversational LLM, Jev doesn’t generate sentences — it returns a “typed decision” with an attached probability, chosen from a schema the developer defines in advance. Because the output shape is fixed ahead of time, the company says it can’t produce an answer outside that schema, and because it samples in parallel rather than generating tokens one at a time, it responds far faster.
The company was founded in 2024 by Diogo Almeida, Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng. CEO Almeida previously co-developed reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) at OpenAI and worked on InstructGPT, ChatGPT and GPT-4.
TypeSafe AI said it closed an $870 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Sequoia Capital and existing investor DCVC participating. The round values the company at $7.5 billion — a jump of dozens of times its seed-round valuation in under a month. a16z general partner Martin Casado is joining the board.
Rather than spell out a spending plan, the announcement stuck to a direction: push everything people like about Jev to the extreme, ship more machine-native models, and keep building out the infrastructure for “smart software.” The company says a third of the Fortune 500 are already using Jev and that it has saved production customers millions of dollars — claims that, as with the seed announcement, come from the company itself and haven’t been independently verified.
The competitive picture hasn’t shifted much. When TypeSafe first emerged, Earendil CTO Armin Ronacher — whose company builds the open-source model harness Pi — said Jev was “alone” in its category for now, but that “once people know this works, competitors will show up.” A month later, no direct rival in the same category has clearly emerged. The closest alternatives remain inference-acceleration infrastructure that runs existing frontier models faster and cheaper on dedicated chips, and guardrail layers that score LLM outputs after the fact. The sheer size of this round suggests investors still see the category as TypeSafe’s alone to lose.

candidates.text:

Fractile Secures £577M Series C to Scale AI Chip Production
Fractile has raised £577 million in Series C funding as the London-based chipmaker prepares to deploy its inference hardware in data centers by 2027.
Elena Whitmore
·
30 October 2026 09:45
·
2 min read
·
14,436 reads
Google'a Ekle
Fractile , the London-based artificial intelligence hardware startup, has secured £577 million in a Series C funding round. Official filings at Companies House confirm the capital injection, marking the firm's largest fundraising effort to date.
Strategic Capital Allocation
The funding was executed through nine share allotment returns filed between 15 October and 28 October. The breakdown of the equity classes includes:
Series C-1: £147.8 million
Series C-2: £37.4 million
Series C-3: £392.2 million
The allotments reflect a significant valuation surge for the company, which was in discussions earlier this year for a pre-money valuation of approximately $6.5 billion. The total raise, when converted, equates to roughly $774 million.
Hardware Ambitions
Founded in 2022 by Walter Goodwin and Yuhang Song , Fractile specializes in inference chips designed to accelerate the response times of large AI models. The company aims to reduce the time required for complex AI workloads from one month to a single day by keeping data adjacent to processing transistors.
Market demand is currently driven by a severe scarcity of high-performance compute hardware. Anthropic has already signaled its intent to integrate Fractile technology, placing an initial order valued at $250 million. The hardware is slated for deployment in 2027.
The Road to 2027
Despite the substantial capital backing, the company faces a critical test. Fractile has yet to ship a production-ready chip to customers. The firm previously utilized its Series B funds to establish engineering operations in London , Bristol , San Francisco , and Taipei . The current infusion of cash provides the runway necessary to transition from design to mass manufacturing.
Investors are betting on the firm's architecture to outperform existing solutions. Competition is fierce. Cerebras and Etched have set high benchmarks for valuation in the inference space. Success hinges on Fractile hitting its 2027 delivery targets. The market is watching. The hardware must perform.

Harvey raises $550M in funding round, valuation reaches $15.5B
SaasRise • Oct 1, 2026
Type Venture Funding - Growth Stage
Value $550M
Harvey Company
Legal AI startup Harvey closed a $550 million growth‑stage round on Oct. 1, 2026, pushing its post‑money valuation to $15.5 billion. The capital will fund product acceleration and deeper market penetration as AI‑driven legal tech adoption spikes among law firms.
Harvey announced a $550 million financing on Oct. 1, 2026, valuing the legal‑AI platform at $15.5 billion post‑money. The round, the largest for the company to date, comes as its annual recurring revenue (ARR) sits at $400 million, implying a roughly 14× ARR multiple on the new valuation. ## Deal Terms The funding round was led by a syndicate of venture firms (details were not disclosed) and will be deployed to expand Harvey’s product suite, scale its engineering team, and accelerate go‑to‑market efforts in North America and Europe. The infusion follows a broader surge of capital into AI‑centric SaaS businesses, underscoring investor confidence in the legal‑tech vertical’s growth trajectory. ## Market Context Recent ILTA survey data show that 40 % of law firms prioritized generative AI over any other technology in the past year, with cloud SaaS applications trailing at 25 %. Within that AI landscape, Microsoft Copilot leads usage at 76 % of firms, while Harvey is adopted by 43 % of respondents, ranking just behind Copilot, Claude (44 %), and Thomson Reuters CoCounsel (44 %). Token consumption on Harvey’s platform has risen 14‑fold in the last six months, reflecting both deeper integration into legal workflows and the looming shift from subscription‑based pricing to consumption‑based models. The funding positions Harvey to double‑down on its open‑weight model strategy, compete directly with the newly launched OpenAI Astra for Law and Google Gemini Enterprise for Legal, and potentially lock in enterprise contracts before the market pivots to token‑based pricing. As law firms grapple with legacy on‑prem accounting systems—still present in 52 % of firms—the move toward cloud‑native, AI‑enhanced solutions like Harvey could accelerate the displacement of traditional software stacks, reshaping the competitive dynamics of the legal‑tech ecosystem.
Why It Matters
Harvey’s fresh war‑chest enables it to outpace rivals in product velocity, particularly against Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude, which currently dominate law‑firm AI usage. By expanding its model‑training capabilities and bolstering its token‑pricing infrastructure, Harvey can lock in higher‑margin consumption revenue, pressuring competitors that remain tied to subscription models. For Thomson Reuters, which is investing $40 million in its own legal LLM, Harvey’s scale and market share intensify the race for data‑rich, open‑weight models, likely prompting faster feature roll‑outs and pricing adjustments across the sector.
For investors, the deal validates the premium placed on AI‑enabled SaaS platforms that address high‑touch, regulated verticals. The 14× ARR multiple signals that capital markets are willing to bet on deep‑stack AI integration as a defensible moat, setting a benchmark for future legal‑tech valuations and influencing fund allocation toward similar vertical AI plays.
Key Points
Harvey raised $550 million, lifting its valuation to $15.5 billion.
Post‑money ARR stands at $400 million, implying roughly a 14× ARR multiple.
40 % of surveyed law firms identified generative AI as their top technology focus.
Harvey is used by 43 % of firms, trailing only Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Thomson Reuters CoCounsel.
Token usage on Harvey’s platform grew 14‑fold over six months.
Analysis
The $550 million raise places Harvey at a $15.5 billion valuation, translating to an approximate 14× ARR multiple—well above the typical 6‑9× range for high‑growth SaaS. This premium reflects the market’s appetite for AI‑first platforms that can embed deep learning models into regulated workflows, where switching costs are high and data moats are defensible. As law firms accelerate AI adoption, the shift toward token‑based consumption pricing could unlock higher gross margins for providers that master usage analytics and cost‑control. Harvey’s capital will likely fund model‑training infrastructure, expanding its open‑weight AI stack to compete with OpenAI’s Astra for Law and Google’s Gemini Enterprise for Legal. For investors, the deal underscores a broader trend: vertical AI SaaS firms are attracting mega‑rounds at multiples that reward both revenue growth and strategic data assets. The financing also raises the bar for comparable legal‑tech startups, pressuring them to demonstrate scalable token economics and robust enterprise pipelines to justify similar valuations. In a market where legacy on‑prem systems still dominate, Harvey’s cloud‑native approach could accelerate the displacement of entrenched vendors, reshaping the competitive landscape and setting a new valuation benchmark for AI‑driven legal SaaS.

candidates.text:
In Brief
Posted:
11:51 AM PDT · October 21, 2026
Image Credits: Big Event Media / Stringer / Getty Images
Dominic-Madori Davis
Legal AI startup Legora raises $550M Series E at $8.8B valuation
Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion.
The company helps automate and assist with workflow tasks for legal professionals, as the industry moves beyond AI assistants to AI services that help them get work done.
The news comes just a month after Harvey, Legora’s biggest competitor, announced a $550 million raise at a $15.5 billion valuation; back in March, Harvey also said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was more than $ 200 million.
Legora’s Series E follows the company’s April announcement of a $50 million extension of a $550 million Series D round, which valued the company at $5.6 billion. At the time, the company said its ARR had reached $100 million. That number now stands at over $200 million, the company shared on Wednesday.
Investors in the latest financing include Atreides Management, which led the round, as well as Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo, and other top names. The company plans to use the fresh capital to further expand across North America.

candidates.snippet: Five robotics startups raise $510M as investors chase physical AI Dealroom
candidates.text:
Fundraise Oct 14, 2026, 22:43 UTC
Five robotics startups raise $510M as investors chase physical AI
What's the deal? Five robotics startups — ICON , Mecka AI , MMI , Multiply Labs , and Ultra — raised a combined $510 million in the week of October 12, spanning construction, surgery, data training, drug manufacturing, and warehouse automation.
The biggest round: ICON, which builds 3D-printing construction robots, raised a $200 million Series D co-led by Baillie Gifford and funds managed by BlackRock . It plans to build a new R&D center, develop new construction systems, and expand its US footprint.
ICON has worked with the Department of War since 2020 on military housing and public infrastructure. It has won more than $370 million in government contracts and built more than 270 homes.
Who else raised? MMI, which makes robotic tools for micro- and supermicro surgery, secured a $125 million Series D led by BioStar Capital Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → . It has deployed nearly 50 of its Symani systems worldwide, used in more than 3,500 surgeries, and will fund US expansion.
Multiply Labs raised a $75 million Series B led by NantWorks for robots that manufacture cell and gene therapies. It sells systems directly to customers, letting them own their supply chain in a heavily regulated industry.
Mecka AI, which builds hardware and sensors to collect egocentric data for training robots, raised a $60 million Series B led by Sequoia . That came four months after $60 million across two undisclosed rounds in June. The company says it is on track for $300 million in run-rate revenue by year-end, after crossing $100 million in June.
Ultra closed a $50 million Series A for two-armed warehouse robots that pack and sort orders. Unlike its peers, Ultra leases hardware monthly, with software supplied through a partnership with Physical Intelligence .
Why now? Training data is in high demand among investors, and specialised robots — for surgery, drug manufacturing, and construction — are moving from labs into regulated real-world use.
The signal: The week's deals skipped general-purpose humanoids entirely, a reminder that capital is flowing across the full robotics stack — from data pipelines to task-specific machines — not just the flashiest category.

candidates.text:
Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal
By Eugene Demaitre | October 30, 2026
Digit 5 includes redesigned legs and new batteries for commercial use. Source: Agility Robotics
Humanoid robotics developers continue to raise millions of dollars. Agility Robotics Inc. and Churchill Capital Corp XI today said that they expect Agility to raise about $465 million in its proposed merger with the special-purpose acquisition company, or SPAC.
According to Agility, the gross capital raise includes:
About $164 million from Churchill XI’s trust account
Approximately $201 million from a common stock PIPE (private investment in public equity) committed at $10 per share, led by Foxconn with participation from existing and new institutional investors
$100 million of equity funding already received following the announcement of the business combination
That total is less than the $620 million that Agility predicted at a $2.5 billion valuation when it first announced the planned business combination in June. The Robot Report has reached out to the company for comment and will add it if we get a response.
“Agility is expected to enter the public markets well capitalized to execute its planned investments in commercial expansion and support growing customer demand,” stated the Salem, Ore.-based company .
Agility expects to close the SPAC transaction, subject to shareholder approval and the customary closing conditions, on Nov. 4. The company has claimed that it will be the first U.S. publicly traded, pure-play humanoid supplier with commercial deployments.
Agility gets Digit ready for customers
Last month, Agility unveiled its Digit 5 humanoid, which had new legs (and possibly wheels ) and is designed to work safely alongside people and support a range of workflows. Last week, Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer, and Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at the company, spoke about humanoid advances at RoboBusiness 2026.
Agility this month also chose Nyobolt for fast recharging, which it said will enable its robots to operate for more than 20 hours a day.
The company said it is “on track to begin deliveries to early-access customers in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of 2027.” Agility also said it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5.
Humanoid use cases are growing
Digit continues to make progress in live operations. In a September S-4 statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Agility reported $1.8 million in net sales in 2025. Its customers across nine sites include Toyota , Mercado Libre , and Schaeffler .
AGCO this month announced plans to deploy Digit in its agricultural machinery factory in Kansas.
And this week, Agility said it is expanding its partnership with GXO Logistics, implementing humanoids in North Carolina and Tennessee.
Humanoid companies continue fundraising, acquisitions
Agility’s investors include NVIDIA (with whom it also expanded its relationship), Amazon, SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Schaeffler, Foxconn, Abico, DCVC, and Playground Global. The company said that all existing shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company and will be subject to a 180-day lock-up at closing.
Some of the top funding rounds for humanoid companies so far this year include Neura Robotics ‘ $1.4 billion Series C, XPeng Robotics ‘ $900 million Series A, AI 2 Robotics ‘ $735 million Series C, and Apptronik ‘s $520 million Series A-X.
Top acquisitions include UBTECH ‘s purchase of Fenglong Electric for $249 million and Faraday Future ‘s purchase this week of FF Robotics.

Stord Secures $400 Million Credit Facility Led by Citi to Scale Its Network, Robotics, and AI Investment, Expands Leadership Team
News provided by
Stord
Oct 08, 2026, 09:30 ET
Share this article
Share this article
Oversubscribed at nearly double the company's original target and joined by Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and others. The financing arrives alongside two executive appointments: Bill Zerella as Chief Financial Officer and Mark Wayland as Chief Revenue Officer.
ATLANTA , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stord , the physical intelligence layer for independent commerce, today announced a $400 million credit facility led by Citi and joined by Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, alongside First Citizens, Citizens, and KeyBank. The company saw significant demand, closing the facility oversubscribed at nearly double the amount Stord originally went to market seeking.
The facility, combined with Stord's $250M Series F at a $3B valuation earlier in 2026, gives Stord substantial liquidity and financial flexibility as the company continues to grow, launch, and expand rapidly. This capital will fund Stord's rapid expansion of its fulfillment network, accelerate the automation and robotics work underway at Stord Labs, and deepen the commerce software and AI that brands rely on to grow revenue, reduce costs, and delight their consumers.
A key investment behind Stord's Series F and credit facility is Stord Labs, the company's physical intelligence lab at its Atlanta headquarters, which tests, develops, and deploys agentic robotics and AI across the Stord network on a single unified stack. That same team embeds forward deployed engineers directly inside Stord's own operations and its customers' businesses, and the results are already showing up in speed and accuracy across the network. With this new capital, Stord will further accelerate its investment in AI and automation across the network.
The financing is announced alongside two executive appointments. Bill Zerella joins as Chief Financial Officer. Zerella has led finance at three public companies, all of which he brought to the public equity markets, including Fitbit's IPO in 2015, where the company grew from roughly $300 million to more than $2 billion in revenue and reached a market capitalization of approximately $12 billion. He most recently served as Chief Financial Officer at ACV Auctions (NYSE: ACVA ), a $1 billion-plus business combining software, fintech , marketplace sales, and vehicle logistics. He understands brands the way Stord's customers do, and he has spent his career building finance inside complex, physical AI businesses like Stord's own.
Mark Wayland joins as Chief Revenue Officer. Wayland brings more than three decades of enterprise sales and revenue leadership, most recently as Chief Revenue Officer at Box (NYSE: BOX ). Before Box, he was Chief Revenue Officer at Tanium and spent more than a decade at Salesforce, rising to Senior Vice President of the Marketing Cloud. He has built global and enterprise sales organizations at public software companies throughout his career.
Stord is approaching $1 billion in revenue run-rate, has grown 10x over the past four years, and has secured $650 million in equity and credit capacity just in 2026 alone.
"Stord is transforming commerce. Our industry-leading scale, fulfillment infrastructure, commerce technology, and applied AI and robotics have rapidly separated Stord as the leader. This facility, combined with our $250 million Series F, gives us the balance sheet to match the scale, potential, and impact of what we're building. We will use this capital to expand our fulfillment network, accelerate our deployment of robotics, and invest aggressively in AI through Stord Labs. The banks in this facility, and the leaders joining us in Bill and Mark, are both a vote of confidence in the foundation we've created at Stord, as well as a signal of where we are headed," said Sean Henry, CEO and Co-Founder of Stord.
About Stord
Stord is the physical intelligence layer for independent commerce. Stord provides the fulfillment network, commerce software, AI, and applied robotics that brands need to compete on the quality of their direct consumer relationships, from the delivery promise shown at checkout to the return that converts into a repurchase. That's how Stord helps brands grow revenue, reduce costs, and delight consumers. Through Stord Labs, Stord is advancing the physical intelligence layer that makes its network faster and smarter with every order. With nearly 100 fulfillment locations worldwide, more than 1,000 brands, and over $15 billion in GMV processed annually, Stord's packages touch one in four U.S. households every year. Stord is headquartered in Atlanta, GA. For more information, visit stord.com .

Reed Jobs’ Yosemite Raises $350 Million to Support Cancer Research
What if the next major breakthrough in cancer treatment is still sitting inside a university laboratory, waiting for the funding needed to move forward?
For Reed Jobs , the son of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs , the future of cancer care may depend on finding those discoveries early, supporting scientists willing to pursue unconventional ideas, and turning promising research into treatments that can reach patients.
Now, his cancer-focused venture capital firm, Yosemite, has closed its second fund at $350 million, marking a major step in its mission to make cancer a non-lethal disease within our lifetime.
The fundraising milestone was reported by Fortune on November 4, 2026, following an interview with Jobs in which he described the fund as oversubscribed, exceeding its original fundraising target.
The new capital brings together major pharmaceutical companies, research institutions, and technology investors around a model that combines traditional biotech venture capital with philanthropic funding for early-stage science.
Among Yosemite’s investors are Amgen , AbbVie , the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) , Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center , and venture capitalist John Doerr .
But the ambition behind the fund goes beyond investing in the next successful cancer drug. Yosemite wants to change how promising scientific discoveries are identified, financed, and ultimately translated into cancer treatments.
From a Personal Loss to a Mission Against Cancer
Reed Jobs’ interest in oncology began long before he entered venture capital.
His father, Steve Jobs, was diagnosed with a rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor and died in 2011. During his father’s illness, Reed began working in cancer research laboratories, an experience that helped shape his professional ambitions.
Rather than pursuing a career in technology, he focused on an equally complex challenge: reducing cancer mortality.
In 2023, Jobs founded Yosemite as an independent investment firm after spinning it out of Emerson Collective, the organization established by his mother, Laurene Powell Jobs .
Its central objective is deliberately different from the often-repeated ambition to cure cancer.
Jobs believes the more realistic long-term goal is to transform cancer from a frequently fatal disease into one that can increasingly be detected early, treated effectively, and managed over time.
Speaking during an October 28 episode of Fortune’s Term Sheet podcast, he summarized his motivation:
“The victory over death. That is what I want for cancer patients.”
Jobs has pointed to the transformation of HIV treatment as an example of how advances in medicine can dramatically reduce mortality from a once frequently fatal condition.
The analogy does not mean that all cancers can follow the same therapeutic pathway. Cancer encompasses hundreds of biologically distinct diseases, each presenting different challenges in detection, treatment, resistance, and recurrence.
Nevertheless, the goal highlights a growing emphasis in oncology on extending survival, preventing cancer-related deaths, and improving patients’ quality of life.
A $350 Million Fund With an Unusual Investment Strategy
Yosemite’s second fund represents a substantial expansion of its investment capacity.
The firm closed its first fund in 2024 with approximately $263 million. In January 2026, Yosemite had secured an initial $200 million toward its second fund’s $350 million target.
By November, the firm had completed the fundraising, creating additional capacity to support emerging oncology companies and research-driven technologies.
What makes Yosemite’s approach distinctive is its combination of two funding mechanisms.
The first is traditional venture capital. Yosemite invests in biotechnology companies with the potential to develop commercially viable diagnostics, therapeutics, and other technologies that improve cancer care.
The second is philanthropic research funding. Through a donor-advised charitable vehicle, the firm supports scientific ideas that may be too preliminary or uncertain to attract conventional investors.
In a July 2026 interview with TechCrunch , Jobs explained that approximately one-third of Yosemite’s venture investments are directed toward companies it helps create, including businesses developed in collaboration with academic researchers.
The remaining venture capital supports companies established by other founders.
He also described a funding arrangement under which 2.5% of the firm’s fund assets under management is directed toward its donor-advised charitable vehicle, alongside $1 million annually from management fees.
The philanthropic and commercial components have different objectives, but they are designed to complement one another: early grants can help establish whether a scientific concept is promising before substantially larger investments are required.
For cancer researchers, that approach could create an additional pathway between basic laboratory discoveries and the development of new treatments.
More Than $18 Million Already Deployed in Research Grants
Yosemite’s philanthropic strategy is already operating alongside its venture investments.
According to an official announcement published on February 12, 2026, the firm had deployed more than $18 million in research and healthcare grants through its donor-advised charitable vehicle since launching in 2023.
The funding supports early scientific investigations, translational research, and projects aimed at improving cancer care.
In the announcement, Jobs emphasized the importance of supporting discoveries before they are commercially viable:
“Academic seed funding is essential to the evolution of cancer care.”

Infinigence AI raises record 2.3b yuan in Series C funding round
By ZHENG YIRAN in Shanghai | chinadaily.com.cn
Updated: 2026-10-14 13:24
Share - WeChat
Xia Lixue, co-founder and CEO of Infinigence AI, delivers a speech during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference 2026 held in Shanghai in July. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn]
Infinigence AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence-native infrastructure company, completed a 2.3 billion yuan ($343.7 million) Series C funding round on Monday, bringing its total funding since establishment to 4.3 billion yuan.
Both figures set records for single-round and cumulative fundraising in China's AI-native infrastructure sector, according to investment consulting firm ChinaVenture.
Founded in 2023 as a technology commercialization venture associated with Tsinghua University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Infinigence AI has attracted investors spanning state-backed funds, industrial investors and financial institutions. Its investors include Lenovo, Tencent, Baidu, HongShan Capital, Qiming Venture Partners and Shunwei Capital, alongside other investors.
The company focuses on connecting computing resources, AI model inference and industry applications through an infrastructure strategy it calls "Agentic Infra". Its framework comprises a computing resource hub, a token production platform and an AI productivity platform serving enterprise customers.
The company's computing platform has access to 37,000 petaflops of computing capacity and supports 16 types of mainstream chips, according to the company. It has also developed a heterogeneous computing platform designed to support large-scale model training across different chip architectures.
In July, Infinigence AI introduced a new inference architecture at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference. The company said the system reduced time to first token by 51.5 percent and could lower the cost per token by 37.5 percent.
Its agentic MaaS (model-as-a-service) platform recorded a 40-fold increase in daily token calls by July compared with December 2025, while the company said technical improvements had reduced inference costs by tenfold over the past year.
Infinigence AI has worked with major Chinese model developers, including Zhipu AI and Moonshot AI, and has developed infrastructure solutions for sectors such as healthcare, energy, legal services and entertainment.
As demand for AI inference grows, the company is seeking to improve computing efficiency and lower deployment costs while helping businesses translate AI capabilities into practical applications.

ASI has raised $325 million in a Series C funding round that values the company at $3 billion . Spark Capital led the financing, with participation from affiliates of Citadel Securities, Meritech Capital, Craft Ventures, Energy Impact Partners and Andreessen Horowitz.
Formerly known as Air Space Intelligence, ASI develops simulation and monitoring software designed to help operators anticipate disruptions across complex systems, including air traffic, electricity networks and military operations. The company said it will use the new funding to expand deployments in energy, logistics and defence, while growing its research and engineering teams in Boston.
The funding follows two major US government awards in 2026: a 12-year, $875 million contract with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), announced in June, and a five-year Army contract with a maximum value of $99 million , awarded in September and announced publicly in October. ASI moved its headquarters from Silicon Valley to Boston in 2024 and changed its name from Air Space Intelligence. What Does ASI’s Software Do?
ASI builds software that models how physical systems are likely to behave and monitors them as conditions change. The aim is to let operators act before disruptions spread, whether that means congestion across an airspace, stress on an electricity network or a constraint in military logistics.
Delta Air Lines, Alaska Airlines and United Airlines use its systems, and the FAA, the US Army and the US Air Force are government customers. ASI also says it is collaborating with National Grid to deploy operational AI on the electricity grid, and that its software supported more than 4,000 US Air Force operators during Operation Epic Fury.

Armadin Raises $255.5 Million Series B to Scale Effective Autonomous Security
News provided by

Oct 01, 2026, 06:00 ET
Share this article
Share this article
Funding brings Armadin's valuation to over $2.5 billion just seven months after its launch as AI compresses the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation
PALO ALTO, Calif. , Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Armadin, an AI-native cybersecurity company building effective autonomous security, today announced it has raised $255.5 million in Series B funding co-led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and Accel that brings the company's valuation to over $2.5 billion. The round includes participation from new investors Bain Capital Ventures (BCV) and Redpoint. Existing investors 8VC, Ballistic Ventures, Google Ventures, In-Q-Tel, Kleiner Perkins, and Menlo Ventures also returned, reflecting their continued confidence, bringing Armadin's total funding to $445 million.
Seven months after emerging from stealth, Armadin is running agentic attack campaigns in production for Fortune 500 enterprises and government customers. As frontier AI models compress the time between vulnerability disclosure and working exploit, periodic penetration tests cannot keep pace. Scanner output fails in a different way, because it scores each finding in isolation. Armadin deploys an autonomous swarm of specialized agents that reason like a skilled adversary across the attack surface, chaining individually low-severity weaknesses into validated kill chains. Those chains run from unauthenticated remote code execution at the perimeter through lateral movement to full cloud compromise. Enterprise and government security teams see the exact attack paths an adversary would use in production today, along with the blast radius of each, and sever them before they are exploited.
"Offense is uniquely advantaged right now," said Kevin Mandia, CEO of Armadin. "AI lets an attacker find and chain weaknesses faster than any human team can respond. The only way to build a defense that keeps pace is to train it against the best offense available, every day. That is what we built. With a16z and Accel co-leading and the support of every investor in this round, we are going to put that offense to work for the enterprises and government agencies defending the world's most critical systems."
Armadin will use the investment to scale its agentic security platform, and to scale its research, training, and go-to-market efforts.
"Against agentic adversaries, the best defense is a great offense powered by AI. That was our conviction when we led Armadin's Series A, and it's even more pressing today," said Ping Li, Partner at Accel. "In less than a year, Armadin has set the standard for AI-powered offensive security and remediation across enterprises and governments, and we're excited to keep partnering with them."
"Every major platform shift creates a new generation of security leaders, and AI is the biggest shift we've seen," said David George, General Partner at Andreessen Horowitz. "Kevin has been on the front lines of the most consequential breaches in history, and he has built a team that pairs elite red teamers with world-class AI engineers. We invested because we believe Armadin will become the defining security company of the AI era."
About Armadin
Armadin is an AI-native cybersecurity company delivering the definitive offensive security platform to identify and eliminate an organization's exploitable risks. As the threat of AI-driven threats escalates, Armadin empowers enterprises to proactively secure their environments. Armadin's platform safely delivers the most comprehensive and powerful AI Hyperattacks to identify new and novel attack paths before adversaries can exploit them. Led by CEO Kevin Mandia, Armadin is a group of engineers, researchers, and hackers on a mission to create effective autonomous security.
For more information, visit www.armadin.com .

Atomic Machines Emerges from Stealth with $250 Million to Launch the Matter Compiler, an AI-Native Manufacturing System That Builds Micro-Machines from Code
Its first product is PrimeSwitch, a previously unbuildable power relay that opens in microseconds for the 800-volt power systems of AI data centers
Atomic Machines today emerged from six years in stealth to introduce the Matter Compiler , the first in a new class of AI-native, all-digital manufacturing systems that build working machines directly from code. The Matter Compiler is aimed at micro-machines: motors and gears the size of a grain of sand, robots small enough to work inside the body, cooling built directly into the chips that run AI, and the many devices like them that have been waiting on a way to build them. The company also announced PrimeSwitch, the first micro-machine produced by the Matter Compiler: an electromechanical power relay that opens in 50 microseconds, about a thousand times faster than a conventional contactor, with no sacrifice in conduction efficiency.
Atomic Machines was founded by Jeff Holden, who joined Amazon as its tenth engineer, built Amazon Prime and rose to senior vice president, then became Uber's first chief product officer and founded its self-driving, AI labs and air-taxi divisions. The company has raised $250 million to date from investors including OneIM, Gigafund, XTX Ventures, KAS Venture Partners, Valor Equity Partners, Tru Arrow Partners, Construct Capital, Sozo Ventures and the Regents of the University of California. PrimeSwitch will be shown publicly for the first time at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, October 12–15.
A gap in how the world makes things
Conventional manufacturing (casting, molding, machining) hits its limits in the low tens of microns. Below that, the dominant capability is semiconductor fabrication, built to do one thing extraordinarily well: pattern flat electronic circuits in silicon. The MEMS industry has coaxed about a dozen commercial device categories from that toolset, among them accelerometers, gyroscopes and micro-mirrors, but under the field's own maxim, "one product, one process," each new device class takes years of custom process development. The result is that micro-machines, one of the most promising unexplored frontiers in hardware, have been blocked not by physics but by manufacturing.
Two breakthroughs
The Matter Compiler brings two breakthroughs to that problem. First, it is a general-purpose constructor: a single system in which code alone determines the device produced, building complete, functional, three-dimensional machines with moving parts, many materials and assembled subsystems, with features down to single-digit microns, and with no hard tooling of any kind. No new manufacturing process has to be engineered for a new device. Second, the entire physical manufacturing system sits inside the AI's loop: every operation is measured with high-precision metrology and corrected in real time, and the AI runs its own experiments on its own hardware to test what simulation proposes. Design intelligence and manufacturing were built together.
"3D printing made shapes programmable: any geometry, straight from a file. We're making machines programmable: many materials, moving parts, sealed and wired, straight from a file," said Jeff Holden, founder and CEO of Atomic Machines. "When the marginal cost of a new design is the cost of the design file, you get an innovation explosion, and micro-machines are where that explosion has been waiting to happen."
"AI has made it almost trivial to create software: say what you want and it exists. The physical world has not taken that leap, because manufacturing was never built for it. The Matter Compiler will let anyone describe an arbitrary micro-machine in code and get a working device out the other end. If vibe coding is how software gets made now, this is the start of vibe manufacturing. Enabling a world with that kind of creativity and abundance is why Gigafund invested in Atomic Machines," said Luke Nosek, Managing Partner at Gigafund.
Rewriting manufacturing economics
Manufacturing wisdom holds that flexibility trades against economics: low unit costs come from committing to tooling and a fixed process, and every design change reopens that bill. Because the Matter Compiler requires neither, its flexibility and its economics arise from the same property rather than competing with each other. A lot size of one carries no engineering charge and no process development. At volume, the same fab that builds one design builds any other, so capital is amortized across every product ever run on it. High-mix and high-volume production happen in the very same fab.
PrimeSwitch: the first micro-machine out of the Matter Compiler
PrimeSwitch was chosen as the company's first product six years ago, from first principles. Power density in electrical systems has risen for a century and will keep rising, and the two technologies for controlling that power each hit a wall. Semiconductors switch fast but lose energy as heat in continuous conduction. Electromechanical relays and contactors conduct almost losslessly and can open a true gap, but they take milliseconds to do it, and at high power they open into an arc. AI data centers, now moving to 800-volt DC distribution to feed racks of unprecedented power density, have made that gap acute: at those voltages a fault delivers destructive energy in microseconds and burns as an arc that direct current will not extinguish on its own. With the new financing, Pigment will keep enhancing Graphite to be able to manage even larger and more complex workloads, while advancing its agents from constructing models and analyzing data to running planning workflows end to end, according to the release.
