candidates.text:
Funding
Warp Sciences Emerges From Stealth With $215M for AI-Powered Chemistry Labs
Published
October 22, 2026
By
Evan Mercer, AI Startups & Venture Capital AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Co-Founders: Kevin Weil (CEO), DJ Patil (COO), Sol Reisberg (Chief Scientific Officer), and Mano Paluri (CTO).
Designing a promising molecule is only the beginning of drug research. Someone still has to make it, test it, and turn the results into a better next experiment. Warp Sciences is betting that this physical bottleneck is where AI can create its next major advantage.
Warp Sciences has emerged from stealth with $215 million in funding to build a U.S.-based chemistry contract research organization, or CRO, combining experienced chemists, AI, and robotics. Led by former OpenAI Chief Product Officer Kevin Weil, the company plans to provide research compounds to biotech and pharmaceutical customers while building laboratories that learn from the experiments they perform.
Lightspeed led the financing, with participation from IVP , Mayfield , Lux , Premji Invest , and Menlo Ventures , among others. Angel investors include Brian Armstrong, Mike Krieger, Dylan Field, and OpenAI’s Mark Chen and Sarah Friar.
A Chemistry Services Business Built Around AI
Warp’s starting point is lead optimization analog synthesis: making variations of molecules so researchers can compare them as they work toward a drug candidate. It is a concrete service with a deliverable, rather than a promise that an AI model will independently invent a medicine.
According to its customer services page , Warp is focused on preclinical small-molecule programs, producing compounds at milligram to multi-gram scale. The company describes its typical work as elaborated molecules requiring five to 15 synthetic steps. That scope places it inside the repeated cycle of making and evaluating compounds that research teams need to refine a program.
Warp also makes a clear distinction about ownership of the research agenda. Customers choose which molecules to pursue and retain control of their drug programs. Warp has no proprietary drug pipeline of its own. Its business is supplying the chemistry and experimental infrastructure those teams use.
That matters commercially. A CRO has to deliver usable compounds, maintain quality, and collaborate effectively with customer scientists. Those requirements give Warp’s automation effort an immediate operational test: whether it makes the service more productive and dependable.
From Laboratory Results to Better Models
The longer-term technology thesis is a feedback loop between experimentation and machine learning. Physical experiments produce evidence about what works. AI systems learn from that evidence, help guide subsequent experiments, and support increasingly automated laboratory work. More capable labs can then produce more useful evidence.
In its founders’ manifesto , Warp says it plans to capture both successful experiments and failures. Alongside customer work, it intends to run dedicated experimental campaigns to generate data for its models. Experienced chemists will lead the laboratories as more of the workflow is automated.
Including failures is an important part of the approach. Knowing that an experiment did not produce the desired result can help define the limits of a method and inform what should be tried next. For that information to improve a model, it needs to be recorded with enough experimental context to distinguish an unproductive idea from a problem in execution.
Robotics supplies the physical side of the loop, while software connects planning, execution, and recorded outcomes. Building those systems alongside the laboratory gives Warp the opportunity to design automation around the work chemists actually perform. The proposed advantage comes from improving the entire experimental process, rather than speeding up molecular design while leaving the lab queue unchanged.
Warp’s broader ambition is scientific AI that can help scientists reason about the physical world and design informative experiments. Its announced commercial starting point remains narrower: delivering research compounds and progressively automating the work required to produce them.
Four Founders Bridging Chemistry, AI, and Operations
Kevin Weil , co-founder and CEO, most recently served as Chief Product Officer and Vice President of Science at OpenAI. His role brings experience translating advances in AI into products and operating systems around them.
Co-founder and COO DJ Patil was the first U.S. Chief Data Scientist and a founding executive at Devoted Health. Co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer Sol Reisberg previously held medicinal chemistry leadership roles at Terremoto Biosciences. Co-founder and CTO Mano Paluri was a vice president at Meta Superintelligence Labs and a founding member of FAIR.
The combination reflects the work ahead: building AI systems, running scientific operations, and delivering chemistry customers can use. Warp says its early team also includes robotics experience from Genesis, Skild AI, and 1X, alongside scientific expertise from Genentech and Lawrence Livermore National Labs.
Charging for Compounds Delivered
Warp’s pricing approach adds another dimension to the funding story. Its website says the company charges per compound delivered, with pricing agreed in consultation with the customer. If a compound is not produced, the customer does not pay for it. Warp contrasts that arrangement with CRO contracts based on full-time-equivalent staffing.
That model connects revenue to completed work. If automation reduces the effort required to make a compound reliably, Warp could improve its own economics while giving customers a more direct connection between spending and output. The company is positioning its service around domestic collaboration and control at offshore pricing, although it has not published a general price list or comparative cost results.

Ledgebrook raises USD 200 million in primary equity financing co-led by Allianz X to scale AI-native specialty insurance platform
News provided by

Oct 07, 2026, 08:00 ET

Funds will scale Ledgebrook's tech-led approach to U.S. specialty underwriting, covering custom and complex insurance needs
Ledgebrook on track to surpass USD 1 billion in cumulative premium written since it started writing business in 2023
Investment expands Allianz X's U.S. property and casualty (P&C) platform into mid-sized general liability risks in excess and surplus (E&S) market
Allianz Re agrees to enter a multi-year reinsurance agreement with Ledgebrook
BOSTON and MUNICH , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ledgebrook, the AI-native specialty insurance platform, today announced it has raised USD 200 million in primary equity financing co-led by Allianz X, the strategic investment arm of the Allianz Group, and Rockefeller Capital Management. Existing and new investors also participated. Ledgebrook will use the funds to scale its technology and extend Blackbird, Ledgebrook's proprietary AI-native underwriting platform. Separately, Allianz Re has agreed to enter a multi-year reinsurance agreement with Ledgebrook.
Continue Reading
Gage Caligaris, founder and CEO, Ledgebrook and Dr. Nazim Cetin, CEO, Alllianz X
Headquartered in Boston, Ledgebrook sits between the brokers who need cover for hard-to-place risks and the capital that backs them, running on technology it built from the ground up. It writes general liability, professional liability, and specialty cover for mid-sized-market businesses in the E&S market, distributed exclusively through wholesale brokers. Ledgebrook's proprietary AI-based platform, Blackbird, reads submissions, classifies risk, and calculates a technical price, quoting specialty risks, often in hours rather than weeks, with experienced underwriters making the final decision. As such, brokers, and therefore their clients, get fast, reliable answers on placing risks. Ledgebrook's approach has put it on track to surpass USD 1 billion in cumulative premium written since it started writing business in 2023.
Gage Caligaris, Founder & CEO of Ledgebrook, said : "Our vision is for Ledgebrook to be the company that makes the wheels of insurance spin faster. Businesses with complex risk deserve specialized underwriting, rated with rigor and delivered at speed. Our platform lets our underwriters do that with real discipline. Allianz X backing gives us the capital to keep investing in technology and talent. We're building this company for the long term."
Dr. Nazim Cetin, CEO of Allianz X, said: "The industry is applying AI to its simplest risks first, because that is where automation comes easily. We think the larger prize sits at the other end, in complex, hard to place business, where underwriting judgment is scarce and slow decisions cost the most. That's exactly the gap Blackbird is built to close, and it's why Ledgebrook fills a meaningful space in our U.S. P&C platform."
John Mullen, President of E&S at Ledgebrook, added : "E&S is seeing strong multi-year growth. Admitted carriers tightened their appetite and pushed risks that were once routinely placed in the admitted market into this channel, and we're excited about accelerating the delivery of value to our distribution partners and insured customers in this segment."
This investment both scales and diversifies Allianz X's U.S. P&C platform, which is built across various lines of business and segments from micro to mid-sized. Ledgebrook writes general liability in the mid-sized segment of the E&S market, filling a meaningful gap on the platform, deepening Allianz's presence in that space, and complementing Allianz X's existing positions.
About Ledgebrook:
Ledgebrook is an AI-native specialty insurance platform. It sits between the brokers who need coverage for hard-to-place risks and the capital that backs them, running on proprietary technology it built from the ground up. Founded in Boston in 2022 by Gage Caligaris, a Harvard mathematician and actuary, Ledgebrook writes general liability, professional liability and specialty coverage through wholesale brokers. In August 2026, AM Best assigned its carrier, Ledgebrook Specialty Insurance Company, a Financial Strength Rating of A- (Excellent) and a Financial Size Category of VIII, completing Ledgebrook's transition to a full-stack platform. The company employs around 300 people, including some 80 underwriters and 50 engineers.

By making and actively managing high-conviction investments in companies with exceptional growth potential and forging unique partnerships between them and Allianz, Allianz X enables transformative collaborations, builds platforms, and unlocks value for the Group.

candidates.title: Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear
candidates.snippet: Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey had an idea to genetically engineer war dogs for the U.S. military, law enforcement, and other emergency response teams. On Thursday, that idea came out of stealth as Warhound , backed by $200 million in funding from investors including Sequoia, 8VC, Corner Ventures, and In-Q-Tel, a venture firm backed by the CIA and other U.S. intelligence agencies. The round values the company at $1.2 billion.
Warhound’s dogs, which do not exist yet, will take on tasks that are dangerous for humans or difficult for machines, such as bomb detection, searches, and other specialized operations. In its launch announcement, the company said that more than 80% of the U.S. military’s working dogs come from Europe, and less than half of them are fit for service.
That means the supply of working dogs is dwindling, and the U.S. increasingly relies on foreign nations for dogs that play an important role in the military and in law enforcement. Warhound aims to change that. The hope is that Colossal can use its technology to engineer dogs with “characteristics suited to demanding missions,” the company said in a press release.
Lamm told TechCrunch he met Luckey about a year ago at a conference, where Luckey said more should be done for the military’s working dogs. The two kept in touch, and Lamm researched how working dogs are bred. He learned that many of them do not make it through training because of inherited predispositions to problems like poor eyesight or the high possibilities of cancer, hip dysplasia, or muscle atrophy.
Lamm believed dogs could be enhanced for health, longevity, and “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot,” he said. His team studied top-performing working dog breeds — the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd — taking cell lines (living cells grown in a lab) from them and putting them in a biobank. From there, the team will edit the dogs’ genes, adding ones that will improve performance and removing ones that will not, to create “a new type of dog.”
Anduril, meanwhile, will provide software and hardware, such as protection vests and goggles, to assist the dogs and their handlers with situational awareness and coordination. Lamm said to imagine, for example, bulletproof vests with data sensors that send information back to the handlers so they can better understand what is happening.
“The idea is, if we make the dog safer, make it healthier, make it perform better, it’s going to perform better in the line of duty,” Lamm said. He added that Anduril’s additions will make the dogs safer and healthier beyond their genetics, “on top of the dog, not in the dog.” He believes the enhancements will also better protect the dogs’ human handlers.
Luckey is a partner in the venture but owns no equity in it, Lamm told TechCrunch. Colossal owns equity in the business and supports it by licensing its technology.
Colossal is currently known for its de-extinction efforts to bring back animals like the dodo and the mammoth . As Lamm previously told TechCrunch, the company has been using AI, buying and building technology to help with gene cloning and with identifying and copying animal genes.
Lamm said the first batch of dogs is about to be cloned and incubated, with births expected early next year and service ideally beginning within two years. Viagen, another Colossal-owned company, will partner with Warhound to clone the dogs. Lamm said Viagen’s technology has a high cloning success rate, and Colossal already uses it in its program to protect endangered species.
Warhound doesn’t know yet how much it will charge for the dogs, but it expects to sell to first responders, the Department of Defense, military service groups, and police forces. Asked about government approval, Lamm said the company has briefed many government groups about the business.
Asked about civilian safety once genetically enhanced dogs enter service, Lamm said each dog will be trained like any military working dog and managed by whoever buys it.
The company said it is working under the guidance of the American Humane Society to help certify Warhound’s training program for the new dogs. The hope is also that when these new military dogs retire, they will enter the Society’s Military Working Dog Reunification Program, which provides homes for retired military dogs — or another program the Society offers to help dogs.
When reached for comment, the American Humane Society said, “We applaud Warhound and Colossal for inviting the country’s first national humane organization, which is grounded in science and ethics, to have a seat at the table. We look forward to working with them to help ensure the animals in their care are treated humanely.”
This piece was updated to add Corner Ventures as an investor and to add the statement from the American Humane Society.

candidates.title: Supabase raises another $150M to build the backend for AI coding from Singapore
candidates.snippet: Supabase raises another $150M to build the backend for AI coding from Singapore Asia Tech Review
candidates.text:
Supabase raises another $150M to build the backend for AI coding from Singapore
New funding comes months after $500M raise and includes strategic acquisition
Jon Russell
Oct 05, 2026
7
1
Share
Welcome back to Asia Tech Review, your curated digest to keep up to date with tech news across Asia.
Supabase might just be the best example of a new tech startup in Singapore. It has built a fast-growing and global business that’s been backed with over $1 billion from investors across the world. And it’s building core tools for the agentic era. Today, we look at its newest round, an acquisition and its future goals.
To keep up with our issues, follow us on LinkedIn or WhatsApp . Please do share Asia Tech Review with people you know who want to get smart about Asia tech.
For news as it happens, follow ATR Bulletin , our real-time news site that keeps you in the know.
The tech startup blueprint Singapore wants to see more of
Supabase, the Singapore-based database platform that helps developers build apps and software, closed a $150 million funding round , just four months after it announced a $500 million Series F round.
The round is led by GIC, the Singapore sovereign fund, and it includes Google’s CapitalG fund for the first time. That’s notable as one of the main competitors of Supabase’s developer stack is Google-owned Firebase. Still, Supabase CEO Paul Copplestone said the fund’s “connections to the broader Alphabet ecosystem will be invaluable as we build for our next level of growth.”
You don’t typically see a smaller round like this follow a huge raise like Supabase’s Series F, but in this case the startup’s recent growth spurt is such that it appears to need the funds to support continuing to accelerate its trajectory.
“Supabase is now adding more than 1M users and 4M databases per month with 70% of new databases created by agents or AI-driven tools. The growth follows a 600% year-over-year increase in databases reported in June, when agents were already deploying the majority of new databases on the platform,” the company wrote.
Supabase has raised over $1 billion in total from investors that include Accel, Peak XV, Craft, Coatue, Y Combinator, Stripe, Salesforce Ventures and Figma.
It’s worth recalling what Supabase does. It provides a set of backend tools to enable developers to quickly build and develop apps, websites and other software using a central resource to manage files, authentication, databases and more. In the agentic era which allows software to be created in minutes or hours not days, that’s a particularly key tech stack as Supabase’s numbers seem to show.
That explains why, alongside the funding round, it announced that it acquired a startup called Turso , which allows databases to be provisioned on demand. That makes perfect sense for Supabase since vibe- and agentic-coding is sending its numbers skyrocketing, it needs the tools to support faster creation of databases and the plumbing beyond apps, websites and more.
Whether you create a web app for friends, a private CRM tool for your company or a new product for an existing customer base, Supabase wants to make its tools the go to for Claude, ChatGPT or bots like Muse, Grok Bot or Dots.
Singapore’s sovereign wealth funds are doubling down on AI startup investments
Jon Russell
·
Jul 10
Read full story
Supabase is the closest example to a modern Singapore tech success story. Its founders aren’t Singaporean, but they met in the country during a cohort for Entrepreneur First.
They didn’t start their business in EF, the accelerator programme that left Singapore in 2023 , but they’ve grown a multi-billion dollar startup from the country without being limited to serving Southeast Asia or raising only from VCs in the region. Speaking of fundraising, you’d imagine that association has helped it win the continued support of GIC, which has been a key backer.
Now, Supabase has a real chance to put Singapore on the map for growing a global business in the age of AI.
India takes down Bitchat, Jack Dorsey’s app used by political protesters
Chat apps are a tough market to enter. There are hundreds of competitors and you need critical mass for a user to find value and return. Bitchat, the messaging app co-developed by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has managed to beat the odds since its launch a year ago. Proof of that comes after it was removed from app stores in India .
Unlike other messaging apps, Bitchat uses Bluetooth to enable chat between devices meaning it can function without cellular signal or WiFi. That led to its popularity surging in India after it was used by protesters over the summer. Its features enabled the protesters, from a Gen Z-led group , to continue to communicate despite authorities cutting access to mobile networks in the area.

12:23 PM · Oct 3, 2026 · 1.34M Views
1.58K Replies · 2.25K Reposts · 13.1K Likes
The Indian government ordered its removal from Apple and Google’s app stores due to illegal content, but it’s fair to assume that’s linked to the protests. That’s proof Bitchat works exactly as intended, though Dorsey would doubtless prefer it remains fully accessible in India. Android devices will allow it to be sideloaded, but no longer being available in app stores will impact distribution.

AI data centre boom brings new demand for old tech
The insatiable demand for AI is making those who provide the key pieces for data centres think outside the box.
Toshiba, for example, has pledged to spend nearly $400 million by the end of next year to double the capacity of its hard drive production in the Philippines. Hard disk drives have long been obsolete for consumers with solid state drives replacing them. But they remain a cheap way of providing storage, which makes them useful in the AI data centre rush.
Another Japanese company is repurposing a technology that never made it off the ground.

Arlington maritime startup raises $140M in Series B funding
Quartermaster AI CEO Neil Sobin. Photo courtesy Quartermaster AI
Arlington maritime startup raises $140M in Series B funding
Quartermaster AI previously announced $43M raise in May
Beth JoJack
// October 5, 2026 //
Listen to this article
SUMMARY:
Quartermaster AI raised $140M in round led by Insight Partners
Round included $40M venture debt facility from Stifel Bank
Company plans to use funding to hire engineers, add vessels to network
Arlington County maritime startup Quartermaster AI raised $140 million in a Series B funding round led by New York-based global software investor Insight Partners, according to an announcement made last week.
Founded in 2023, Quartermaster AI was launched to fix what it calls “the largest blind spot on Earth.” The shipping and maritime industries, the company maintains, are operating on incomplete data because building real-time sensing infrastructure for an area as big and dynamic as the ocean is cost-prohibitive.
Led by CEO Neil Sobin, Quartermaster AI’s solution is equipping the world’s 6 million vessels already sailing the world’s oceans with SmartMast, an onboard sensing and edge-compute platform.
The round included participation from Overmatch Ventures, a Texas firm that makes early stage venture investments in critical technologies, defense and space, and returning investors First Round Capital, a California venture capital firm that works with founders at the earliest stages of company building; Steel Atlas, a New York investment firm; Quiet Capital, a California firm that specializes in early stage investments across the United States; and TMV, a New York venture capital firm that backs early stage founders in legacy industries.
Missouri’s Stifel Bank provided a $40 million venture debt facility, a type of loan designed for early stage companies, according to a Sept. 28 news release.
Insight Partners Managing Director Nick Sinai said in a statement: “Quartermaster is building a distributed network for the ocean, where reliable, real-time data has been difficult to come by. The team’s execution and the strong demand for maritime data and awareness made this an investment we wanted to lead, and we’re proud to back Neil and the team as they scale to meet the opportunity with commercial fleets.”
This round of funding wasn’t Quartermaster AI’s first of the year. In May, the company announced it had raised $43 million in Series A funding co-led by First Round Capital and Quiet Capital, with participation from TMV; Steel Atlas; BoxGroup, a New York early stage investor; Oper

Mavria raises $130 million to mass-produce modular AI data centers
Photo: Brett Sayles / Pexels
The Houston-area startup, backed by Paradigm, AMP PBC and others, wants to build data centers in a factory instead of on site
by
Diego Almada Lopez
Mon 9 Nov 2026 · 13:12 EST
·
3 min read
In Technology
Share

Data centers have traditionally been built like custom homes: one site, one design, one long list of headaches. Mavria wants to build them more like cars coming off an assembly line.
The Houston-area startup has raised a total of $130 million to scale manufacturing of its factory-built data centers. That includes a $100 million round led by Paradigm, which puts the company at a post-money valuation of $1 billion .
Unicorn status on launch day
Mavria launched on November 9, 2026. It arrived with a billion-dollar price tag and a product already on the production floor.
Paradigm led the round, but it brought company. The backer list also includes AMP PBC, Critical Frontier, Liquid 2 and Dream Ventures.
The founding trio comes from an unusual place for a hardware startup: the US Department of Energy. CEO Adam Blake, Seth Cohen and Nick Poradek all previously worked at the agency.
The company’s first product line is called Terrain. Each unit is a standardized 5 MW block that bundles power, cooling and IT infrastructure into a single package.

The blocks are designed for high-density artificial intelligence workloads. The first unit, Terrain 01, is currently in production in Houston. Mavria has not disclosed which customers will deploy Terrain or where the units will go.
Why build a data center in a factory
The pitch is about repeatability. Conventional data center construction is site-specific, which means every project gets designed and built more or less from scratch.

Mavria’s bet is that AI infrastructure should move toward an industrialized model. Design one block, perfect it, then build it over and over.
The company frames the approach as a way to speed up AI infrastructure rollout. That rollout is currently running into two stubborn walls: power constraints and construction constraints.
Standardized blocks attack the construction problem directly. If most of the work happens on a factory floor, less of it has to happen on a muddy job site.
The 5 MW unit size also matters. Modular blocks theoretically let an operator add capacity in increments rather than committing to a single giant build all at once.
The investor lineup tells its own story
A $100 million lead check is a strong signal at any stage. The supporting cast adds weight too. AMP PBC, Critical Frontier, Liquid 2 and Dream Ventures all joined Paradigm on the cap table.
Still, a $1 billion valuation before any disclosed customer deployment sets a high bar. Investors are pricing in the factory’s future output, not its current one.
What this means for AI infrastructure
Factory output alone does not solve the power problem. A finished 5 MW block still needs 5 MW of electricity waiting for it at the destination.
That is where the founders’ energy policy experience may prove useful. Navigating grid access and energy infrastructure is a skill set, and this team spent time where those decisions get shaped.
The things to watch are fairly concrete. First, when Terrain 01 leaves the Houston production line and where it ends up. Second, whether Mavria names its first customers. A disclosed deployment would turn a promising pitch into a proven product. Third, how quickly the company can move from a single unit to repeatable volume. Raising $130 million to scale manufacturing means the scaling part now has to actually happen.

candidates.text:
← Deals
AI SaaS Venture Capital B2B Growth
Clay raises $115M in Series D funding round at $7.1B valuation
SaasRise • Oct 2, 2026
Type Venture Funding - Series D
Value $115M
Clay Company
Clay, the AI‑powered GTM infrastructure startup, closed a $115 million Series D round in September 2026, lifting its post‑money valuation to $7.1 billion. The financing follows a rapid growth trajectory that saw ARR triple to $100 million and an employee tender offer at a $5 billion valuation. The new capital will fund product expansion, the emerging GTM‑engineer role, and broader market adoption.
Clay announced a $115 million Series D financing on September 2026 that values the company at $7.1 billion, marking the latest milestone in its AI‑driven go‑to‑market platform rollout. The round, whose investors were not disclosed, comes on the heels of a February report that Clay had tripled its annual recurring revenue to $100 million in a single year and a prior employee tender offer that pegged the firm at a $5 billion valuation.
Deal Terms
The Series D injects $115 million of growth capital into Clay’s product and engineering teams. While the lead investor was not named, the financing round is positioned to accelerate the development of Claygent—Clay’s OpenAI‑powered agent that automates research, data enrichment, and outreach across sales, marketing, and recruiting. The company also unveiled a $1 million scholarship fund to train the nascent GTM‑engineer profession, underscoring its commitment to building an ecosystem around its platform.
Market Context
Since its 2017 launch in Brooklyn, Clay has evolved from a no‑code spreadsheet tool into a full‑stack GTM infrastructure layer. By embedding AI across the revenue stack, it enables teams to replace manual, multi‑tool workflows with repeatable, agentic systems. The rapid ARR growth and soaring valuation reflect a broader market shift toward AI‑augmented revenue operations, where investors are rewarding platforms that can both generate expansion revenue and create new job categories—evidenced by the emerging GTM‑engineer role that Clay coined in 2023.
The Series D capital will fund product enhancements, deeper integrations with data sources, and expansion into adjacent verticals where AI‑driven revenue automation is still nascent. With more than 10,000 founders, investors, and operators gathering at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Clay is poised to showcase its roadmap and capture additional enterprise customers looking to scale growth without proportionally expanding headcount.
Why It Matters
Clay’s infusion of $115 million gives it the runway to outpace rivals such as Cursor, Lovable, and Webflow, which are also courting the GTM‑engineer talent pool. By formalizing a scholarship program and branding the role, Clay can lock in early adopters and create a network effect that makes its platform the default stack for AI‑native revenue teams. Competitors will need to accelerate their own AI integrations or risk losing market share to a solution that already bundles data access, workflow automation, and an OpenAI‑backed research agent.
For operators, the deal signals that building an internal GTM‑engineering capability may no longer be a cost center but a strategic differentiator. Companies that invest in AI‑driven revenue systems can achieve higher net‑revenue retention and lower customer‑acquisition costs, while those that rely on fragmented tools may see margin pressure as the market coalesces around platforms like Clay.
Key Points
Clay raised $115 million in a Series D round, valuing the company at $7.1 billion.
The financing follows a February report that Clay’s ARR grew to $100 million, a three‑fold increase in one year.
Clay’s valuation rose from $5 billion (employee tender offer) to $7.1 billion within months.
The round will fund the Claygent AI agent and a $1 million scholarship to train GTM engineers.
Investors were not disclosed, and the deal was announced in September 2026.
Analysis
The $7.1 billion valuation translates to roughly a 71x multiple on Clay’s reported $100 million ARR, a premium that reflects the market’s appetite for AI‑centric revenue platforms. Investors appear willing to pay for the promise of higher expansion revenue, lower churn, and the creation of a new GTM‑engineer discipline that can embed automation deep into the sales funnel. For SaaS operators, the deal underscores the strategic advantage of shifting from a labor‑intensive GTM model to an AI‑orchestrated one—potentially boosting net‑revenue retention and gross margins while reducing headcount costs. For venture capitalists, Clay’s trajectory validates a broader trend: capital is flowing to vertical‑agnostic infrastructure that can be layered across multiple SaaS categories, from marketing automation to recruiting tech. As more enterprises adopt AI‑driven revenue stacks, we can expect a wave of follow‑on funding for comparable platforms and heightened M&A interest from larger CRM and ERP players seeking to bolt AI‑enabled GTM capabilities into their ecosystems.

candidates.title: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
candidates.snippet: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Technology
October 20, 2026 / TechCrunch News / 0 Comments
SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.
The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.
“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.
And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.
Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.
Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.
The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station.
Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.
“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.
The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)
While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.
“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”

About General Compute
General Compute is a neocloud that rents out AI inference capacity built on specialized chips from Nvidia rivals such as SambaNova, Cerebras, Positron AI and d-Matrix. It buys the hardware and runs it in rented colocation data centers, using Nvidia GPUs to process prompts and the specialized chips to generate output tokens faster. General Compute makes money by selling this capacity to AI companies and inference providers, either as dedicated bare-metal servers or as a guaranteed tokens-per-second service under one contract. candidates.text:
Home
Hardware & Chips
Dream Labs Raises $90M Seed for Any-Robot AI Model [2026]
Tom Vance
Updated Nov 3, 2026 · 17 min read
Dream Labs, a San Francisco startup founded by former Nvidia robotics researchers, came out of stealth on October 19, 2026 and announced that it has raised $90 million in seed funding to build foundation models that can run on robotic hardware from almost any manufacturer. The round, led by B Capital with participation from Kindred Ventures, A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and angel investor Adrian Aoun, is one of the largest seed checks written this year for a company betting that robot “brains” should be decoupled from robot bodies.
Table of Contents
What Dream Labs Actually Announced
How Dream API Is Being Offered
Why Hardware Makers Should Care
The Funding Numbers in Context
How Dream-1 Compares to Other Robot Foundation Model Efforts
Historical Context: Robotics’ Software Problem
Market Impact: What This Means for the Robotics Supply Chain
The Compute Cost Question
What Industry Watchers Are Saying
Risk Factors Investors Are Watching
Predictions: Where This Goes Next
The Bigger Picture for AI Hardware
Frequently Asked Questions
What is Dream Labs?
How much funding did Dream Labs raise?
What is Dream API?
What tasks can Dream-1 perform?
How many hardware partners is Dream Labs working with?
How is Dream-1 different from other robot AI models?
What will Dream Labs use the funding for?
Is Dream-1’s performance independently verified?
Related Coverage
The announcement lands alongside the public debut of Dream API, which Unite.AI reports the company describes as the first commercially available API for a robot foundation model. According to the announcement, Dream API takes a robot’s camera feed plus a plain-English instruction and converts both into motor commands, including on hardware the underlying model has never seen before. For a hardware industry that has spent the past two years chasing custom silicon for AI inference, Dream Labs is making the opposite bet: that the bottleneck in robotics is not the chip inside the machine, it is the software brain that has to generalize across thousands of different chassis, grippers, and sensor rigs.
·
Google · Preferred Sources
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Add now
What Dream Labs Actually Announced
The core of the announcement is Dream-1, a robot foundation model that the company describes as a World Action Model that “controls robots it has never seen, performs tasks it was never shown, and runs from $3/hour,” trained on videos of people performing everyday tasks rather than on robot-specific teleoperation data alone. Dream Labs says the model can handle tabletop tasks such as picking and placing objects and folding laundry, and that it can control bimanual robots fitted with parallel grippers without needing robot-specific training beforehand. That claim, if it holds up under independent testing, is the whole pitch: one model, deployed through an API, working across hardware it was never explicitly tuned for.

More than 20 hardware partners are reportedly already on board, according to Pulse2’s coverage of the funding round , spanning companies that build arms, mobile platforms, and grippers for warehouses, labs, and light manufacturing. Dream Labs has not published the full partner roster, and the company has not disclosed Dream-1’s parameter count, inference latency, the exact list of supported robot models, or reliability rates in real-world deployments. Those gaps matter, because the entire value proposition rests on generalization across unfamiliar hardware, and generalization claims are notoriously hard to verify without a public benchmark or third-party audit.
Dream Labs says the new capital will go primarily toward compute, as the company works to expand the range of tasks and robot types Dream-1 supports and scales up capacity for API users. That is a familiar refrain in 2026’s AI funding cycle, where compute spend has become the default answer to “what will you do with the money,” whether the product is a chatbot or a robot arm, a point RuntimeWire’s reporting on the deal also underscores.

Riemann’s 13.1B-Parameter AI Model Hits Hugging Face [2026]

How Dream API Is Being Offered
Alongside the model, Dream Labs launched Robot Playground, a browser-based experience allowing users to send commands to a robot in the company’s San Francisco office and observe the result remotely. Dream API itself was described as live for everyone, though available summaries characterize the service as an experimental research beta. For readers weighing it, the browser demo and the API are the practical ways to test the company’s claims before committing hardware or budget.
The company’s own page ties the pitch to falling hardware costs, stating that a capable bimanual arm setup can now cost as little as $2k. Dream Labs was also reported to work with robots priced roughly between $2,000 and $10,000. To show how the model adapts to a specific machine, the page offers timelapses of data collection on two of its partners’ robots, 5 minutes each, and says that after adapting on just those 5 minutes, “Dream-1 now understands a bit better the affordance and kinematics of the robot.” The page lists Dexmate, Sharpa dexterous hands, 77 minutes of data, and YAM, compliant gripper and modified knife gripper, 98 minutes of data.
For hardware makers, the practical step is to check whether their robot fits the announced scope of bimanual robots with parallel grippers, using camera images, robot state, and a task instruction to prod

candidates.title: Israeli AI publishing co Spines raises $64m - Globes
candidates.snippet: Israeli AI publishing co Spines raises $64m Globes - Israel Business News
candidates.text:
Zeev Ventures, the Palo Alto-based venture capital firm founded by Israeli investor Oren Zeev, is leading another multi-million dollar investment round in Spines , a digital publishing company.
Spines is now raising $29 million in equity from Zeev Ventures, Aleph, Dan Senor, and other investors, alongside $35 million in debt financing from Twelve - a new debt fund established by the Galai brothers, cofounders of Outbrain. While the company’s valuation for this round has not been disclosed, it is understood that it has not yet reached the $1 billion mark.
Two years ago, Spines closed its Series A funding round; at that time, its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was $3.5 million, with total revenue for that year reaching $5 million. Today, the company’s ARR is $50 million, with 8,000 authors in its portfolio who have collectively published over 12,000 books.
Spines caters to thousands of amateur authors, willing to pay for self-publishing, who are not served by traditional publishing houses (which fully or partially fund the works of about50,000 professional authors annually). Authors upload their manuscripts to the platform, where the company’s AI agents edit and proofread the text, design the cover, and handle the book’s layout. Spines then distributes the titles across the market, including platforms like Amazon and Barnes & Noble, in digital, audio, and print formats. To avoid holding inventory, the company prints physical copies only when an individual order is placed. Audiobooks can be produced using a library of available voices, or by sampling the author’s own voice to train an AI model to narrate the story on their behalf.
Spines does not accept books written by AI. The company employs technology specifically designed to detect AI-generated content. However, for an additional fee, users can hire a human editor to enhance the quality of their writing. The company currently serves the English-speaking market, while also enabling the translation of books from English into Spanish, Italian, French, German, Portuguese, Polish, and Hebrew. Translations are generated using AI and then reviewed by professionals for whom the target language is their native tongue. Over the next six months, the company plans to expand its service to 20 languages.
"In the US alone, there are about 50,000 professional authors who publish their books through established publishing houses like Penguin and Simon & Schuster; yet, around 2.5 to 3 million new books are published annually," Niv tells "Globes". "The vast majority of these books - 99% - do not succeed in terms of sales. Publishers recoup their investments through the 1% that do become successful. We target a different market: amateur authors, publishing a book for the first time, who might otherwise approach established publishing houses only to be presented with a bill ranging from $10,000 to $150,000. Our typical package costs between $5,000 and $7,000 and within two weeks, these authors have a book of their own."
Unlike large publishing houses, Spines is a commercial publisher that does not necessarily seek "bestsellers" and does not employ manuscript readers. Consequently, the company does not finance the publication of books for talented authors. Nevertheless, the company takes pride in having around 100 authors who have successfully sold several thousand copies of their books.
Spines was founded in 2021 by CEO Yehuda Niv, CSO Lev David, CTO Nir Kenner, and CPO Niv Ovdat. In 2013, Yehuda Niv founded Niv Publishing, which releases over 1,200 titles annually. The company has 350 employeesa including 90 based at its offices in Herzliya, and the remainder in the US, Eastern Europe, and South America.
Oren Zeev said, "When Yehuda first told me what he wanted to build, Spines was still in its early stages. Two years later, I saw that he and his team had built exactly what he described, and the company is growing rapidly. This is precisely what I look for in entrepreneurs. I was one of the early investors in Audible, and I witnessed how innovative technology could transform a long-established market like the book industry. I believe Spines has the opportunity to bring about a similar shift in how books are published."
Aleph cofounder Michael Eisenberg added: "Having written and published nine books, I am well-acquainted with the journey that begins once a manuscript is finished. It is a long, costly, and complex process, requiring coordination with numerous professionals. When we invested in the company during its seed round, we saw an opportunity to leverage AI to make this process faster, more efficient, and accessible to many. The company’s growth since then demonstrates a genuine demand for this. To me, the great opportunity lies in opening up the world of publishing to more people - to a wider array of compelling voices and original ideas."

candidates.title: Ultra raises $62 million for fast-growing ‘robots as a service’ business, announces tie-up with AI research firm Physical Intelligence
candidates.snippet: Ultra raises $62 million for fast-growing ‘robots as a service’ business, announces tie-up with AI research firm Physical Intelligence Fortune
candidates.text:
Finance editor Jeff John Roberts here. The explosive growth of the robotics industry in recent years is reflected in new technology feats, but also by the proliferation of new business and distribution models. Ultra, a startup that leases its devices to warehouses under a monthly “robots as a service” model, is a case in point. On Friday, the Brooklyn-based company announced it had raised $62 million, while also deepening a partnership with the buzzy “robot brains” AI firm Physical Intelligence.
Recommended Video
Ultra’s funding came in two rounds: a $50 million Series A led by Framework Ventures with participation from Y Combinator, and an earlier $12 million seed round led by the latter and Next View.
In an interview with Term Sheet, Ultra CEO and co-founder Jon Miller Schwartz made a point we’re hearing a lot these days: Namely, he says humanoid robots get the lion’s share of attention, but that it is other forms of robots that are having the most impact in the real world. This phenomenon is hardly a new one: Recall how, in the 1980s, fictional robots like C3PO and Terminator’s T-800 captured the popular imagination, even as people gave little notice to new robotic arms doing actual work in auto factories.
Today, humanoid robots have made their way from the movie screen into real life, but they are prone to falling over, and their makers are struggling to deploy them in everyday situations. Ultra’s robots, on the other hand, can be found in warehouses across the country and according to the company, the devices have packed more than half a million orders for shipping.
Unlike many Silicon Valley engineers, Schwartz studied mechanical engineering, which means he and his team spend their days doing hands-on stuff with metal parts, cables and motors. That includes going to so-called 3PL (third party logistics) sites, and installing Ultra’s robots that specialize in packing goods for transit.
Ultra’s contraptions are part of a growing robot empire taking over the country’s warehouse and logistics operations. Notable players in the space include France-based Exotec , whose robots specialize in climbing vertical racks to retrieve things and, of course, Amazon and its fleet of devices working alongside humans in hubs across the U.S. There is also Uber founder Travis Kalanick, who is also firmly in the non-humanoid robot, and who recently stepped back into the public eye with a plan to complete what he started at the ride-sharing firm. Kalanick’s new company, Atoms, is a massive logistics and AI play that he says will one day use one robot to cook your burrito and another to bring it to your door.
While Ultra is riding a wave, its early success has come in part from its shrewd as-a-service business model. Schwartz says the company has booked significant revenue (he didn’t disclose how much) because Ultra doesn’t require customers to lay out large amounts of capital to use its robots. Instead, clients pay an up-front integration fee for Ultra to install the robots, and then an ongoing monthly fee for ongoing hardware and software support. The model has gotten so much traction that Schwartz says Ultra has been able to raise prices.
There is a second intriguing part of Ultra’s business model, which is its decision to employ what some call the “body and brains” approach to robots. That means Ultra builds and installs the robots, but relies on Physical Intelligence to supply the AI that allows them to learn and improve rapidly in response to any given customer’s set-up. Numerous other robot makers are also using software from PI, which is valued at $5.6 billion, and was founded by a team from Google DeepMind who published a landmark paper on robotic intelligence.
The tie-up between Ultra and Physical Intelligence thus reflects a clever division of labor and distribution play—one that lets the former focus on its core robot-building competency, while PI gets out-of-the-lab data to better train its models. As for when we’ll see this sort of scaling on the humanoid robot side of things? Schwartz says give it five years.
See you Monday,

TeddyHoldings.AI Raises $60 Million in Seed Funding from Leading Investors to Transform Compliance and Client Service in Legal Services, and Announces Over $25 Million in Revenue
TeddyHoldings.AI (“Teddy AI”), a compliance and client-focused legal services platform incubation, today announced it has raised $60 million in Seed funding from leading investors and passed $25 million in revenue. Teddy AI is a partner-oriented legal services vehicle with the sole mission of providing its clients and constituents with the best possible support across compliance and performance. The company is keeping its specific focus, leadership, and cap table confidential for now.
The U.S. legal services industry generates roughly $400 billion of revenue a year – more than a third of a global market of over $1 trillion – spread across tens of thousands of firms, many of which serve clients that require a high degree of compliance and care for client information and end customers.
The compliance and client-focused legal services platform was incubated by Tucker’s Farm Corporation (“Tucker’s Farm”), a value-oriented holding vehicle that has grown into a family of companies across industries and geographies. Tucker’s Farm aims to acquire $100-$200 million of long-term assets every year as it seeks to find and compound cash flows through highly active M&A and reinvestment strategies in the lower-middle market (and still boasts a strong herd of ~20 Nubian half-pygmy goats in its legacy cheese-mongering business).
Kyle Tucker, founder of Tucker’s Farm Corporation’s private equity arm, remarked:
“We’re keeping lots of details stealth-ish for now. But Teddy is not an AI company - it’s a compliance and client-oriented legal services platform. Our sole mission is supporting our clients and we’ll use technology to the extent it helps that endpoint. And to grossly generalize - we think most law firms are tough businesses - key man risk, project-based revenue, a ton of AI risk etc. So, I think we’re skeptical of general legal theses. By ‘most law firms’ I’m referring to undifferentiated general purpose corporate law firms that draft documents and give advice etc.”
Tucker continued:
“Separately, we’ve now spent too much time on ‘AI rollups’ and have increasingly strong views on what’s real and real-ish and what’s jazz hands. Today I think some things are real. Tomorrow, I think most things are real (maybe everything? I’m usually a pretty even-keeled ‘reversion-to-the-mean’ type of guy but looking at the progress, it’s hard not to be full ‘tin-foil-hat’ regarding AI capabilities in the long term and increasingly in the medium term). But our bigger issue is it’s still not super clear to us what an average ‘AI rollup’ can uniquely do vs another ‘AI rollup’ in the same sector, or even vs an enterprising non-AI-native rollup for that matter. Meaning, yeah, AI margin expansion is real in some rollup categories but most of it seems achievable by resourceful competitors (with off the shelf or easily buildable tools). So, the big question for us is still – if you’re AI native (or an AI early adopter), how much margin do you uniquely keep at the end of the day? We’ve only found one or two real secrets.”
On where Tucker’s Farm sees the real opportunity, Tucker added:
“But man, we’re so excited about AI for anything kind of verifiable, especially if you don’t need low-latency inference (i.e., you’re okay with slow but super smart). For instance, as we think through our rollup investment function, we can’t help but feel that the traditional ‘investment guy/gal’ is in trouble. Which I think is a meaningful statement, because I was a traditional investment guy (!) at Apollo (PE) and Viking (HF). But right now, we’re getting probably the equivalent of a week of Blackstone PE associate underwriting work in like one hour of model run time and $50 of tokens (granted using intensely curated harness/weights/context/etc. that we’ve spent all summer building and powering that with frontier class intelligence - Fable and a little Astra right now but constantly benchmarking accuracy across our models and across our underwrites).”
He went on:
“More generally, AI sort of feels like COVID in its ubiquity - impacting everything in the collective consciousness and general zeitgeist - so we welcome any applied AI engineering talent that wants to join!”
Regarding the Seed funding cap table, Tucker said:
“We’re staying quiet regarding our cap table but it’s a lot of traditional Limited Partners (endowment manager, etc.), anchored by awesome multiple-repeat past partners. We opened fundraising calls for 3 weeks and got about $115 million of varied equity asks and closed on $60 million for the Seed. It’s our strong belief that equity sizing (‘equity efficiency’) is the name of the game for high MOIC outcomes. But we’ll revisit sizing for Series A depending on reinvestment needed.”
Regarding Tucker’s Farm Corporation, Tucker said:
“We’re a reinvestment focused holding vehicle. Meaning we’re looking for high returns on capital. A lot of the time this is via M&A (‘rollups’, ‘buy-and-builds’, ‘aggregations’, ‘serial acquisitions’ – choose your language etc.) or de novos (‘green-fields’, ‘newbuilds’ etc.), but increasingly we’re more interested in finding more unconventional reinvestment opportunities. I’ll leave it at that. We’ve also added the language ‘AI-oriented holding vehicle’ in our tagline for the Farm. This was originally schtick (on top of our goat farm schtick) – basically a tongue-in-cheek nod to all the AI-rebrands, particu

Marina Temkin
Robot data startup Mecka AI nabs $60M from Sequoia
Mecka AI, a startup that collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots, announced it has raised a $60 million Series B round led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Microsoft’s venture fund M12, and others. TechCrunch had previously reported that the startup was nearing a new funding round at a $500 million valuation.
Founded in 2024, the startup intends to do for robotics what Scale AI, Mercor, Surge, and other data-labeling companies have done for LLMs. Those companies supply the human-generated data these systems learn from. Mecka pays people to record themselves doing everyday tasks, like making coffee or fixing cars, while wearing body sensors and using smartphones.
Other startups that collect real-world data for robot training include XDOF, which was in talks to raise a Series B round at a $1.2 billion valuation according to TechCrunch’s previous reporting. Human-data platforms that began with LLMs are also expanding into robotics, such as Scale AI and Micro1 .

BY Venture Partners raises $60 million to back AI startups
My Startup World Staff
October 29, 2026
Comments Closed
0 like
BY Venture Partners, a global early-stage venture capital firm headquartered in Dubai, today announced the successful $60 million close of its third vehicle, Fund III. The fund is anchored by the Dubai Future District Fund (DFDF), with participation from established regional institutions, corporate venture arms, and prominent family offices, including leading regional player in AI and high-speed data infrastructure Multi Lane, Transmed Capital, and the Idriss Family Office (KSA). Fund III expands BY Venture Partners’s total Assets Under Management (AUM) to over $200 million.
Empowering AI-Native Founders from a Regional Powerhouse
Fund III will invest primarily up to $1m at the Pre-Seed to Series A stages into AI-native companies that reimagine enterprise workflows and scale globally from day one.
Headquartered in the UAE, BY Venture Partners operates from a region embracing AI at a pace. McKinsey’s November 2025 GCC survey found that 84% of organisations used AI in at least one business function, up from 62% in 2023. The firm invests across more than 16 international markets, with two-thirds of its capital deployed outside the MENA region across North America and Europe. Early momentum for Fund III is already underway, with 15 investments deployed to date out of a planned 40-company portfolio, including PQ Shield, Cosyne, Isometric, Huspy and Invisible.
“We are thrilled to officially announce Fund III today,” said Ghaith Yafi, Founding Partner at BY Venture Partners. “The focus of this fund is to back AI-native companies with global ambitions. We are particularly excited about the opportunity to attract some of the world’s most innovative AI companies into the Middle East and connect them with the region’s rapidly growing technology ecosystem. We are executing on a thesis designed to generate strong, long-term returns for our partners.”
Institutional backing for regional impact
The anchor commitment from DFDF reinforces BY Venture Partners’s role in elevating the Middle East as a global tech hub and bridging regional capital with international deal flow.
“We committed to Fund III because BY’s model works in both directions. It brings global AI-native companies into Dubai and takes founders from this region into international markets, and that exchange is what Dubai’s Economic Agenda D33 asks of us. Ghaith, Abdallah, Rami, Sohrab and the team have built and exited companies themselves and have managed capital through a full market cycle. The flow of companies and founders across that bridge is the basis on which we will measure this partnership,” said Nader Albastaki, Managing Director, Dubai Future District Fund (DFDF).
“We have been firm believers in BY Venture Partners since inception, and we are delighted to contribute to the firm’s Fund III, to help back up-and-coming AI-first startups in the region,” said MultiLane Founder and CEO Fadi Daou. “As an ecosystem builder myself, as well as a former entrepreneur, BY’s vision fully aligns with ours.”
Rebuilding Ecosystems: The Lebanese Angel Investor Network (LAIN)
Rooted in a commitment to ecosystem building, BY Venture Partners won the MITAI-backed mandate to manage and operate the Lebanese Angel Investor Network (LAIN). LAIN connects global diaspora capital with early-stage Lebanese founders, creating a structured pipeline for early-stage capital and connecting the next generation of regional angel investors. Demonstrating its long-term commitment to ecosystem recovery, BY will reinvest 50% of its carried interest directly back into rebuilding the Lebanese startup ecosystem.
Built by Founders, for Founders
BY sets itself apart through its operator-first DNA: all four partners – Ghaith Yafi, Abdallah Yafi, Rami Jisr and Sohrab Jahanbani – are repeat entrepreneurs who built and exited businesses before joining forces as investors. This hands-on, founder-centric approach has earned BY Venture Partners a Founder Net Promoter Score of 87.
BY’s track record has been built across more than one market cycle, including a full financial collapse in Lebanon, where Fund I carried significant exposure. That fund is still on course to return a strong multiple to its investors. The fund has had to adapt to fast-changing market conditions and has built a reputation for moving quickly to support founders in their most difficult and challenging days. Fund II continues to perform strongly relative to its vintage. Between them, the two funds have produced four unicorns, two from each, alongside a growing group of companies now valued in the hundreds of millions, and the firm has already returned meaningful capital to its LPs.
With Fund III, BY Venture Partners continues to leverage its global-first, AI-first network to give early-stage founders the operational edge, capital, and global connectivity required to build market-defining technology platforms.

Artificial intelligence (AI) assistant startup Wabi has reportedly raised $55 million in new funding.

The new financing values the company at $1.25 billion and will help it work on its software that lets groups of people interact with AI to coordinate activities and make decisions, Bloomberg News reported Thursday (Oct. 29).
The report describes Wabi as the latest in a series of startups in the personal assistant field, where companies like OpenAI and Meta are vying to draw more users to the AI offerings.
OpenAI last month debuted its agent Dots, which users can interact with via messaging and calls and which was built to conduct work on their behalf. Also in September, Meta introduced its assistant Muse, which quickly garnered more than 10 million downloads .

Wabi, the Bloomberg report added, introduced its latest update Oct. 19. Users can bring the assistant into group chats to help plan trips, line up schedules and manage day-to-day tasks. It can turn conversations into shared tools like travel itineraries, handle requests like booking appointments or making shopping returns.
“AI shouldn’t just save people time. It should help them spend it better, doing more of what they love, with the people they love,” Wabi’s Founder and CEO Eugenia Kuyda told Bloomberg.
Among the investors in the round was Andreessen Horowitz. That firm took part out of a belief that Kuyda has a strong intuition for building AI for everyday Americans, said general partner Anish Acharya . Many other companies, he added, tend to design agents that are “built by technologists for technologists.”
Research by PYMNTS Intelligence has shown the prevalence of AI usage among those everyday Americans.
According to the research from the report “How AI Becomes the Place Consumers Start Everything,” more than six out of 10 consumers said they used a dedicated AI platform in the last year, illustrating the technology’s arrival as mainstream behavior.
More than one-third of Gen Z consumers and Power Users—or those who perform 25 or more AI-driven tasks—now turn to AI first when beginning personal tasks, “marking a clear move away from traditional search and browsing,” PYMNTS wrote.
The research also found that 42% of consumers who primarily use dedicated AI platforms say that they’ve begun using search engines less often, compared with 33% among consumers who mainly encounter AI through search summaries.

0
HardScope Accelerates Rebel Audio's Next Phase of AI Technology, Creator Ecosystem & Global Expansion
Newly Established Board Of Directors includes DraftKings Founder & HardScope CEO Matt Kalish, Ben Lurie, Jacob Dezarn, and Jonathan Schulman alongside Advisory Board Members Mark Burnett and Chief Creator in Residence Mike Majlak
NASHVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rebel Audio, the AI-powered podcasting platform designed to radically simplify how podcasts are created, produced, and scaled, today announced the closing of its Series A funding round, led by creator media company and studio HardScope. The Series A, which immediately follows an initial oversubscribed seed round of $4.15M, targets a $10M close, valuing Rebel Audio at approximately $50M post-money (*with more funding to follow in a 90 day window). The funding will accelerate Rebel Audio's product roadmap, expanding its AI infrastructure, fuel creator acquisition and marketing, and support the company's continued growth as it sets out to build the future of the podcast industry.
Rebel Audio is building an end-to-end operating system for the next generation of podcasters and creators. The platform brings together the tools creators need to record, edit, publish, translate, distribute and monetize their content, while using AI to streamline workflows that traditionally require multiple platforms.
"I started my career in dark editing rooms, fighting the tools just to get the work done, and have been building creator tools ever since," said Jared Gutstadt, Founder and CEO of Rebel Audio. "Rebel is the simplest version of that mission: remove the friction, give creators their time back. Matt co-founded DraftKings and scaled it into one of the biggest names in sports entertainment. He knows technology, and he knows performance marketing. That's the fuel for our network effect."
"Rebel Audio empowers millions of aspiring creators to make great content independently and with almost no friction," said Matt Kalish, CEO of HardScope. "The next generation of creators will use one-stop-shop AI powered platforms to show you don't need a big team to create and launch great content. You can get started today, all by yourself on Rebel's technology. Empowering creators to build ambitious projects and build an audience is core to HardScope's mission."
The Series A follows an oversubscribed seed round that helped take Rebel Audio from stealth to public beta, leading to Rebel's recently announced inaugural creator think tank, POD U, taking place Friday, Oct. 16 at the Rebel Chateau in Franklin, Tennessee. POD U will bring together creators, platform leaders, athletes, media executives and investors shaping the future of media with headline guests including MDMotivator, Mike "Big Mike" Majlak, Rebel Audio's Chief Creator in Residence; Caleb Simpson; Andrew Essex, Fort Nash's Chris Ruediger, the Ecomm Cowboys and more. The event will be moderated and produced by Jimmy Jellinek, the former Playboy and Maxim editor turned public radio producer.
Additional participants and programming details for the first-ever Pod U will be announced in the coming weeks.

Harmonic Security Raises $50M Series B to Expand US and UK Teams
Published
October 14, 2026
By
Evan Mercer, AI Startups & Venture Capital AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Harmonic Security announced on October 14, 2026, that it raised a $50 million Series B round led by Crosspoint Capital Partners, with participation from existing investors. The company said the round, which it described as oversubscribed, brings its total funding to $76 million.
Series B Round and Expansion Plans
In the funding announcement , datelined San Francisco and London, Harmonic said it will use the new capital to expand its engineering and go-to-market teams in the United States and the United Kingdom. The company said it has grown to more than 90 people across the two countries.
Harmonic said it protects and enables AI use for millions of employees at more than 100 companies, including what it describes as some of the largest enterprises in the world. The company also signed new distribution partnerships with Climb and Distology.
“Security has too often slowed the adoption of new technology. As organizations embrace AI, they shouldn’t have to choose between moving quickly and maintaining control,” said Zach Sivertson, managing director at Crosspoint Capital Partners. He said Harmonic gives leaders the visibility and confidence to accelerate AI adoption while employees use the tools that make them more productive, with the right guardrails in place.
Alastair Paterson, Harmonic’s chief executive and co-founder, said the company has real momentum and is just getting started, adding that the round allows it to build faster while continuing to respond to shifts in the AI landscape.
Platform Capabilities and Ecosystem Integrations
Harmonic describes its product as the only platform that classifies every AI task, discovers why it is used, and then controls it in real time. The company said that in the 12 months before the announcement it extended beyond browser-based AI monitoring to cover desktop AI tools and agentic workflows in a single platform, coverage it frames as closing the gap where personal-account use, sensitive data exposure, and other risks tend to start.
The platform is built on custom small language models that, according to the company, read each AI interaction in context and return a result in milliseconds, enough to distinguish a developer referencing a schema from someone pasting live credentials. Harmonic said the same engine powers its Usage Intelligence layer, which shows leaders which AI use cases are creating value, which employees have found a faster way to work, and where to invest next rather than where to clamp down.
“Every board I talk to is asking two questions: how do we reduce the risk of AI use, and are we getting value? Most vendors struggle to answer the first, yet we address both,” Paterson said. He said the company committed to its custom small language models from the start, which he said gives it unique insight into enterprise AI use.
Harmonic is named among the ecosystem integrations for Cisco Cloud Control’s new Agent Builder, announced at Cisco Live, connecting through the Model Context Protocol. Separately, the company built an integration with Claude’s Compliance API, which Harmonic said gives security teams visibility into Claude Platform activity logs and, for organizations on Claude Enterprise, into conversation content across Anthropic-hosted deployments.
Company History and Prior Funding
Harmonic Security was founded in August 2023, according to the company’s About page . Paterson is chief executive and co-founder, and Bryan Woolgar-O’Neil is chief technology officer and co-founder. Ten Eleven Ventures led the company’s $7 million seed round in October 2023, the month the company launched.
The company was named an RSA Innovation Sandbox finalist in April 2024 and launched its Harmonic Protect data protection product in July 2024. On October 2, 2024, Harmonic announced a $17.5 million Series A round led by Next47, with Next47 general partner T.J. Rylander joining the board. Harmonic said at the time that it had secured more than $26 million since launch, that enterprise customers were already in double figures, and that its data protection product was in active use by thousands of employees. The company employed 30 people across the United States and the United Kingdom at the time.
The About page lists the company’s board and investors as Rylander, Bain Capital CISO Mark Sutton, Ten Eleven Ventures founder Alex Doll, In-Q-Tel partner Grant Whiting, and N47’s Colton Dempsey, along with advisor René Bonvanie, CMO emeritus of Palo Alto Networks.
Harmonic launched its MCP Gateway in October 2025 and introduced an updated brand in January 2026.
