candidates.title: Sabi Raises $50 Million Seed Round Led by Khosla Ventures to Put a Brain-AI Interface Inside a Baseball Cap
candidates.snippet: Sabi Raises $50 Million Seed Round Led by Khosla Ventures to Put a Brain-AI Interface Inside a Baseball Cap GlobeNewswire
candidates.text:
Sabi Raises $50 Million Seed Round Led by Khosla Ventures to Put a Brain-AI Interface Inside a Baseball Cap
FinanceWire
Oct. 9, 2026, 12:28 PM
SAN FRANCISCO, Calif., October 9th, 2026, FinanceWire
The non-invasive cap is powered by a custom EEG chip and more than 100,000 hours of labeled neural recordings, which Sabi believes is the largest disclosed dataset of its kind. An early prototype will debut at CES 2027.
Sabi today announced it has raised a $50 million seed round, led by Khosla Ventures, to develop a brain-AI interface designed for everyday wear. Accel, Initialized Capital, former OpenAI Chief Product Officer Kevin Weil, DST Global, Collaborative Fund and Ascend also participated.
Sabi’s first product looks like an ordinary baseball cap. Sensors hidden inside it read neural signals through hair without gel, surgery or direct contact with the scalp. Sabi is developing the cap to translate imagined speech and intent into commands for AI.
Brain-computer interfaces have largely been designed for clinical settings and cursor control. Sabi is pursuing a different use: giving people a faster, private way to communicate with AI without typing or speaking.
AI systems can now write, research and take action, but people still direct them through keyboards, touchscreens and voice commands. Implantable interfaces can capture detailed neural activity, but surgery prevents them from becoming an everyday input method. Sabi is developing a non-invasive alternative that can be worn outside the laboratory.
Each cap contains sensors measuring between one and five millimeters, built around Sabi’s custom EEG chip. The sensors are designed to capture signals through hair across a gap of up to five millimeters. In internal benchmarks, the chip was more than 50 times as power-efficient as the Texas Instruments ADS1299, a widely used EEG analog front end. That efficiency allows the electronics to fit inside ordinary headwear while limiting heat and electrical noise.
The neural signals are processed by Sabi’s Brain Foundation Model. The model has been trained on more than 100,000 hours of labeled, non-invasive recordings collected while participants imagined words and performed specific mental tasks. This is the largest disclosed dataset of its kind.
Sabi is developing three primary forms of interaction:
Imagined speech to text. Words a user intentionally imagines can appear on a connected screen without being spoken or typed.
Thought to prompt. A trained mental command can become an instruction for an AI assistant, such as asking it to draft a message or retrieve information.
Intent prediction. The system can anticipate likely keystrokes or on-screen actions and present them for the user to complete or confirm.
The cap connects to a phone or computer wirelessly, much like a pair of earbuds. Sabi plans to demonstrate early versions of these interactions at CES 2027 in Las Vegas.
Neural data is encrypted beginning at the sensor. Sabi’s system is designed to run inference while that data remains encrypted, preventing servers from receiving a user’s unencrypted neural signals. The company is also building user controls around when the cap records, which applications may receive commands and which actions require confirmation.
Sabi was co-founded by CEO Rahul Chhabra and CTO Atmadeep Banerjee. Banerjee is co-first author of MindEye, the NeurIPS 2023 paper that advanced the decoding of viewed images from non-invasive brain recordings. The company’s team includes hardware, machine-learning and design leaders from Kernel, Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Adobe and Nike, alongside neuroscientists from Stanford.
“AI can write, reason and act, yet we still communicate with it by tapping on keyboards and screens,” said Chhabra. “We are building a faster interface that does not require surgery or a laboratory. The goal is a cap people can wear in ordinary life and use when they intentionally want to communicate with AI.”
“You cannot perform a billion brain surgeries to replace a billion keyboards,” said Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures. “Every computing era is defined by its interface. Sabi is building one designed for the age of AI.”
Sabi will use the funding to expand its neural dataset, complete development of its custom chip, manufacture early devices and grow its neuroscience, hardware and machine-learning teams. The company is also preparing units for members of its early-access waitlist.
About Sabi
Sabi is building a non-invasive brain-AI interface for everyday use. Its first device places custom EEG sensors inside a baseball cap and uses a Brain Foundation Model trained on more than 100,000 hours of labeled neural recordings to translate imagined speech and intent into commands for AI. Sabi is backed by Khosla Ventures, Accel, Initialized Capital, Kevin Weil, DST Global, Collaborative Fund and Ascend.
Learn more at https://www.sabi.com/

AI agent security startup AIR raises $50M seed, lands on Fortune Cyber 60
What's the deal? AIR Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , a Tel Aviv-based startup securing enterprise AI agents, was named to Fortune's 2026–2027 Cyber 60 list after raising $50 million across two seed rounds. Sequoia led a $10 million round and Greenoaks led a $40 million round.
What does it build? AIR sells a security layer for AI agents and the ecosystem of add-ons that extend them — skills, plugins, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. The platform continuously vets those components, enforces policies at runtime, and offers a marketplace of pre-vetted add-ons.
Why now? Enterprises adopting AI agents are inheriting fresh risk from the tools those agents access, which can change over time. AIR frames the problem as a supply chain issue rather than one of model access or prompt filtering.
"Approving an AI add-on once isn't enough," said Yair Saban, co-founder and chief executive officer of AIR. "Organizations need to know what their agents are using, whether those components remain trustworthy, and when to revoke access."
About the list. Fortune produced the Cyber 60 with Lightspeed Venture Partners and AWS , recognizing 60 venture-backed cybersecurity startups across three stages of growth. AIR emerged from stealth in September.
What could go wrong? List inclusion is third-party validation, not proof of commercial traction. The open question is whether AIR can convert investor interest into enterprise adoption in a crowded, fast-moving market.
The signal: A $50 million seed is unusually large for a cybersecurity startup, and it reflects where capital is flowing.

Press Release
Hyphenate raises $45M Series A following 86x revenue growth as CFOs move to autonomous finance
October 27, 2026 6 min read
Hyphenate’s customer base grew 11x in 12 months, including six public companies, and its self-learning agents now run 90% of routine finance work across the platform.
Summarize With: Open in ChatGPT Open in Claude Open in Grok
Share Link Book a Call
New York City, NY - October 27, 2026 ; The first wave of finance AI helped teams work faster. The next is taking responsibility for the work itself. Hyphenate , the autonomous finance platform for the office of the CFO, today announced a $45 million Series A led by Nexus Venture Partners, with participation from B Capital and existing investors including Foundation Capital, BoldCap and Gaia Ventures.
Inside Hyphenate customers, agents are already reconciling cash, processing sales orders, running invoicing, maintaining subledgers and moving the close forward, with finance teams stepping in only where judgment changes the outcome. The round, which brings total funding to $54 million, comes less than a month after Maximor rebranded to Hyphenate, as customers expand its use across the office of the CFO. The company will use the capital to take its agents deeper across the finance function and into strategic finance.
“Every finance team carries a long list of work it does because somebody has to,” said Ramnandan Krishnamurthy, co-founder and CEO of Hyphenate . “Our customers are watching that list shrink in production. Once a team sees the system handle one workflow to an auditor’s standard, they hand it the next one. That is the pattern this company is built around, and this round lets us run it across the whole function.”
12 months from seed to 86x
Hyphenate raised a $9 million seed one year ago to take repetitive work off finance teams. Since then, the company has passed multi-million-dollar ARR, its agents have taken on work across hundreds of entities, thousands of bank accounts and millions of transactions every day, and customers report 90% less repetitive finance work and 75% fewer audit exceptions. The more telling number is what customers do next: 40% expand within their first year, several by two to three times, and the average customer runs six modules.Companies are handing the system larger parts of finance once it has proved itself in one workflow.
What that looks like in production
The expansion is now visible in production, at companies where finance errors carry real cost.
Mini Melts USA, the consumer goods company, runs Hyphenate agents on top of its SAP environment for orders, invoicing and refunds. Within three months of going live, the company was getting back 16,640 hours of finance work a year.
HiBid, one of the largest online auction platforms in North America, has run more than $2.5 billion in GMV through full order-to-cash automation on Hyphenate. Invoicing, collections and cash application across that volume now run as a single continuous process, and the company has cut its month-end close from three weeks to one day.
Groupon, the Nasdaq-listed marketplace, is replacing legacy and home-grown systems with Hyphenate across treasury, order-to-cash and more than a dozen subledger processes.
“ As a public company, we run finance at a scale where every number has to stand up to scrutiny: millions of transactions, multiple currencies and markets, and auditors who need the evidence behind all of it. We’re replacing legacy and home-grown tools with Hyphenate because it’s built for that bar, and we see it becoming the AI foundation for our entire finance organization ”
Rana Kashyap
CFO of Groupon
Synthesia, the AI video platform, is rolling Hyphenate out across its finance function.
“ As an AI company, we expect our own operations to run on AI. The breadth of the Hyphenate platform has improved every functional area of our accounting and finance operations. We replaced point solutions with an autonomous finance platform that understands our business. Now the team focuses on exceptions and analysis, which helps make decisions faster, ”
Daniel Kim
CFO, Synthesia
How Hyphenate works
Hyphenate sits on top of the ERP, banks and other systems a company already runs and connects them into a single shared finance context. The business keeps its systems of record and gains a layer that can act across all of it.
On that layer, agents work across five areas of finance: order-to-cash, treasury, GL accounting, procure-to-pay, and reporting and insights. In practice that covers revenue recognition, invoicing, collections, cash reconciliation, accruals, subledgers, AP, close and board reporting.
What sets the system apart is that it’s self learning. Instead of relying on forward-deployed engineers to build bespoke agents for each customer, Hyphenate trains on a company’s historical spreadsheets, emails and system logs, then replays past months to pick up the edge cases traditional software never handled: the tribal knowledge that has kept finance manual. From there, it gets better the longer it runs. An exception resolved during one close becomes precedent for the next. A policy decision made once is applied every time the same situation appears. Every action carries its evidence with it, so the output is audit-ready by default. Month by month, the share of routine work handled autonomously rises, and the finance leader’s involvement narrows to the decisions that require judgment.
The trust threshold is moving
Finance has been one of the hardest functions for AI to enter autonomously. Research commissioned by the company earlier this year found that 96% of CFOs saw freeing teams for strategic work as AI’s biggest benefit, while only 14% completely trusted AI to produce accurate accounting data independently. Ninety-seven percent said human oversight was critical.

candidates.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
candidates.snippet: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache TechCrunch
candidates.text:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.
What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.
“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.
The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium , a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.
She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium.
Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

candidates.title: Healthleap raises $38M for its AI that flags hospital patients who may need a closer look
candidates.snippet: Healthleap raises $38M for its AI that flags hospital patients who may need a closer look TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Healthleap , a startup building an AI platform that reads patient records to identify patients at risk of undiagnosed illnesses, has raised $38 million in seed and Series A funding, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.
The financing includes an $8 million seed round co-led by Sequoia Capital and First Round Capital, and a $30 million Series A led by Hummingbird Ventures. The company is not disclosing its valuation.
Founded in South Africa in 2022 by siblings Jemima and Josiah Meyer (pictured above), the startup initially offered a clinical nutrition tool Jemima had built for dietitians. But the company later pivoted and built a more general-purpose platform that aims to identify patients admitted to hospitals who may be suffering from conditions like malnutrition or delirium that aren’t often identified early enough, CEO and co-founder Josiah Meyer told TechCrunch.
“A patient’s chart holds two kinds of data. Labs, weights, and vital signs sit in structured fields, but the most telling signs sit in clinicians’ written notes: poor appetite, recent weight loss, muscle loss, trouble swallowing. Our developing approach is extracting affirmative or negated mentions of these clinical concepts in an easily extensible and scalable way,” Josiah said.
The company’s platform is currently deployed in more than 50 hospitals, where it screens patients for conditions such as malnutrition and delirium, he said. The startup has also built programs to identify aspiration pneumonia, pressure ulcers, and risk of readmission for congestive heart failure, which Josiah said are undergoing further clinical validation.
To find patients that may be at risk of an illness or were undiagnosed, Healthleap plugs into a hospital’s electronic health record system and uses language models to pull information from written notes, such as references to recent weight loss or difficulty swallowing. That analysis is then fed into its risk models, alongside structured information such as lab reports and vitals to surface patients who may need a closer look. The company notes that its software doesn’t diagnose patients, only highlights items for additional review.
“Each night, we analyze every adult inpatient’s record: lab results, vital signs, weights, medications, diet orders, diagnoses, clinicians’ notes, and more,” Josiah explained. “Each morning, we write a risk score into the care team’s existing workflow with a dashboard accessible that holds additional information about the patients’ trends.”
Malnutrition likely served as a useful starting point for Healthleap, as it’s a condition that often goes undiagnosed and can adversely impact patient recovery in a variety of ways. Research suggests 20% to 50% of hospital inpatients are malnourished, and some studies have linked malnutrition with longer stays, impaired wound healing, infections, and other complications, as well as higher morbidity and mortality.
Josiah said Healthleap has grown from three hospital partners to more than 50 over the past year, and its customers now include Penn Medicine, Cedars-Sinai, Intermountain, Houston Methodist, and Emory Healthcare. Revenue has grown more than 10x over the same period, he said, though he didn’t disclose specifics.
The startup sells three-year contracts priced according to a hospital’s licensed bed count, and also uses an outcome-based pricing model. “We use the hard ROI that the hospital finance team validates and attributes to us as the measurable ROI. Based on that, we contractually ensure that we deliver multiples of the contract price. To date, every customer has seen a 5x hard ROI or more, in some cases over 20x annual total ROI,” Josiah said.
At the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Healthleap says its malnutrition program resulted in $23.8 million in annualized financial impact, of which $6.3 million came from additional reimbursement and $17.5 million from shorter hospital stays.
Healthleap plans to spend the fresh cash on engineering, product, sales, and customer success as it adds support for identifying more conditions. Josiah said the company ultimately wants to cover more than 40 major health conditions and expand into outpatient and home care.

doxx.net Raises $38 Million, Led by Andreessen Horowitz, to Launch Agentic Defined Networking
doxx.net Lets People And Agents Set Up Private Networks So They Can Browse, Mesh, Transfer Files, Call, Video, And Message With No Servers in the Middle
doxx.net , founded by Barrett Lyon, best known for pioneering the DDoS defense industry with Prolexic (acquired by Akamai) and other successful security and networking companies, today launched the open beta of its Agentic Defined Networking (ADN) platform, which lets people and their agents create their own private, secure networks, communicate with no servers in the middle, and get started with no personal information required. The platform gives agents an environment with defined connectivity and built-in threat protection, helping prevent them from reaching known malicious destinations while they browse and act on a user’s behalf. Try it now at doxx.net .
The company also announced $38 Million in Series A funding, led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Animo Ventures and Focal.vc. Joel De La Garza, partner at Andreessen Horowitz, joins the doxx.net board.
doxx.net gives people and their agents a parallel, private network they can build on: browse privately, transfer files directly, connect devices and agents, and communicate peer to peer. The technology is built for everyone, from everyday users browsing privately, to advanced users connecting home networks and agents, to journalists in censored regions reaching the open internet.
"Have you ever had your agents configure your network, lease public IP addresses, and set up your security policy, to then discover you can call your friends through your own private network with no one in the middle? No record of the call? No phone company involved, where your phone is also the server?" asked founder and CEO Barrett Lyon after the first call on the network. "That was our first freedom call."
Built for the Agent Era
AI agents are increasingly browsing, communicating, accessing services, and taking action on behalf of users. That creates a new security problem: an agent can encounter a fake login page, a malware-hosting site, or another malicious destination while operating with its user’s data, accounts, and authority. doxx.net gives people and agents a private, policy-defined networking environment with DNS-level threat protection that blocks known and emerging malicious destinations before an agent or person connects. Since December 2025, doxx.net has blocked more than 38 million threats in closed beta.
Agents on doxx.net get what humans get: their own network identity, private channels to their humans and each other, and the ability to build the network they run on, through a full network API with native MCP support. No other network treats people and their agents as peers on infrastructure one company owns end to end. Have your agent visit https://config.doxx.net to explain it to you.
"The industry sells privacy as a feature while routing your traffic through rented infrastructure they don't own and can't verify," said Barrett Lyon, founder and CEO of doxx.net. "We physically built something different: a platform where privacy comes from the architecture itself, not a policy document. We do that so people and agents using the network, not third parties, set the terms of their privacy. They know what you search, where you go, and who you talk to. We don’t. And we built the network so we never can."
“The internet was never designed for privacy,” said Joel De La Garza, partner at Andreessen Horowitz. “doxx.net has built a one-stop privacy stack from first principles, delivering truly private security and communications capabilities, so humans and AI agents can run on a network that is private by architecture, not by marketing promise.”
Secure Architecture With User Control
Most ‘private networking’ products are just prettier tunnels into public clouds. doxx.net delivers users a parallel, sovereign internet with its own DNS root, IP space, encrypted mesh, and agent-driven networking, so there’s no mystery infrastructure between you and your traffic.
Key benefits include:
Agentic Defined Networking. Allow your agents to set up networks for you, call you, chat with you, lease your own IP addresses, and configure your firewall.
Call, message, and share files directly. P2P Comms connects you through end-to-end encrypted calls, video, chat, and file transfers, with no communications server in the middle.
Let the network quietly catch threats before you ever see them. DNS Protection combines 30 filter lists with a neural network that catches threats no static list has seen, automatically protecting you and your agents from malicious phishing and malware sites.
Stay connected even where VPNs are blocked. Covert Networking uses six protocols designed to make private-network traffic look like ordinary web browsing.
Make it harder for sites to track you. Anti-Fingerprinting masks identifying details about your browser and device to help prevent tracking across websites.
Keep your identity and activity separate by design. Onion routing moves your traffic through multiple servers before it exits, so no single point knows who you are and what you're doing at the same time.
Run on a private network with its own naming system. The Parallel Internet Ecosystem gives you 196 custom TLDs and your own certificate authority, so your network resolves domains the public internet has never heard of, with no third parties.
doxx.net has native apps for iOS, macOS, and Android, with support for Windows and Linux, all running on its global backbone.
Open Beta
Join the open beta, where you are not the product. No email, no phone number, no account required.

What is fintech?
What is fintech?
Fintech, or financial technology, is a term that describes the mobile applications , software and other technology that enable users and enterprises to access and manage their finances digitally.
It is also used interchangeably with the term fintech startup, which refers to a company whose core capability is in the development and/or delivery of fintech products and services.
As smartphones and other digital devices have gained popularity, fintech use cases have increased steadily. Today, popular mobile apps help people set financial goals, apply for mortgages, file taxes and much, much more. At the enterprise level, businesses across the financial industry are constantly on the lookout for ways to deploy fintech to increase their capabilities and offer more products and services to their customers.
The evolution of the term
The term "fintech", a combination of the words "finance" and "technology", was initially used by banks to describe technology that helped them track and manage their clients’ accounts. However, in the last five years, the term has shifted to include more consumer-related services, such as apps and software that are used to create budgets, track spending and buy and sell stocks.
Today, the term fintech can be used to describe technologies, services and companies in the financial sector that focus various capabilities, including retail banking, financial education, fundraising, cryptocurrencies, investment management and more.

Why is fintech important?
As smartphones have crept into more and more areas of our lives, many industries have felt pressure to digitize more of their capabilities and services. From ride-hailing apps and refrigerators that know when you’re out of milk, to virtual classrooms and chatbots , digitization is everywhere you look. Fintech is just another example of an industry (the financial industry) moving steadily into the digital age.
When it comes to digitization, banks and financial institutions started slowly, automating and digitizing processes that had been done manually for years. The ability to open a new account, conduct a money transfer and pay for goods and services online were some of the first breakthroughs.
Today, the pace of innovation has increased to the point where some banks don’t have physical infrastructure at all. Digital banks(or neobanks, as they’re commonly referred to) offer fee-less, digital-only banking options for customers that don’t require a physical location.
Fintech has also helped expand banking into traditionally underserved communities. For example, according to a report by the Brookings Institution , over 90% of Hispanic consumers use fintech, along with 88% of African Americans and 79% of Asian consumers.
Fintech has also played a big role in driving growth, allowing financial institutions to offer certain services 24/7 with the use of chatbots, rather than physical employees. This helps cut down on overhead while still giving customers access to critical services around the clock rather than just during traditional banking hours.

Benefits of fintech
Fintech products and services provide many tangible benefits to both consumers and businesses. For consumers, fintech has brought innovations in the digital payments space as well as new ways to manage and optimize personal finances. At the enterprise level, fintech helps automate and streamline business processes and speed the delivery of new digital products into the hands of customers. Here’s a look at the top three benefits for each audience, starting with consumers.
Top three fintech benefits for consumers
1. Seamless access to finances: One of the biggest benefits of fintech products for consumers is round-the-clock access to their finances. Whether trading stocks, transferring money or making a last-minute purchase, fintech allows users to conduct financial transactions when and how they need to.
2. Highly secure transactions: As the laws and regulations around fintech increase, so do the security requirements fintech applications must follow to be allowed to enter the market. In addition to minimizing the physical theft or loss of a credit card or cash, fintech offers customers robust cybersecurity solutions that protect them from hackers . Blockchain technology , for example, is a relatively new fintech innovation that uses a distributed ledger to ensure the validity of complex, multiparty, online transactions.
3. Increased access to credit: Digital lending—the process of applying for and receiving funds through a digital process—is growing quickly, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of as much as 16.7% according to Allied Market Research . Fintech solutions make it possible for more borrowers to access a wider pool of lenders digitally than they could through traditional financial services channels. Some fintech startups even offer credit to individuals with poor or nonexistent credit ratings.
Top three fintech benefits for enterprises
1. Improved business processes: Fintech capabilities have helped streamline business processes by enabling the automation of mundane tasks associated with banking services. Also, businesses who operate fintech applications have seen their transaction and investment processes significantly speed up when their customers have 24/7 access to their accounts through mobile apps.

Scuba Emerges from Stealth with $34M to Build the Shared Context Engine for Teams and Their Agents
Scuba Emerges from Stealth with $34M to Build the Shared Context Engine for Teams and Their Agents
Provided by Business Wire
Oct 13, 2026, 4:00:00 PM
Scuba Emerges from Stealth with $34M to Build the Shared Context Engine for Teams and Their Agents
Founded by former Slack leaders, Scuba is the shared memory teams have been missing, so they can stay aligned and move smarter together.
Scuba, the shared context engine for teams and their agents, today emerged from stealth with $34 million in funding over two rounds. Accel led the pre-seed, with IVP joining Accel to co-lead the seed. BoxGroup, Conviction, Homebrew, and Scribble Ventures also participated. Scuba’s angel investors include founders of Slack, Instagram, Stripe, LinkedIn, Salesforce, Datadog, Vanta, Harvey, Dropbox, Abridge, Duolingo, Granola, Warp, Zynga, Groupon, Coda, Opendoor, and Flatiron Health.
AI is helping people move so much faster on their own. But few teams feel they are actually moving smarter together. Speed doesn’t add up when the team runs in different directions. Effort gets wasted. Lessons get orphaned. Old alignment tools can’t keep up. The monthly all-hands are too slow. The wiki is too stale. The strategy docs are too long. AI gives teams instant answers. But their competitors get the same ones, averaged from the public internet. No team wants to be average. They have their own point of view.
Scuba is the shared memory every team has been missing. It lets teams capture and share what matters so they can move as one. The context. The thought. The lesson. The plan. Teams can save from their browser, any app, their agents, or directly: the articles, screenshots, docs, videos, threads, texts, voice notes, and write-ups. Scuba organizes it all automatically, tracking the team’s knowledge, decisions, and directions as they evolve. No manual editing required. It works behind the scenes as a proactive thought partner that connects the dots across the team. Teams connect Scuba to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and Slack, so every answer, artifact, and line of code starts from everyone’s best thinking.
Founded by Noah Desai Weiss, former Chief Product Officer at Slack, and Dolapo Falola, former Head of Engineering at The Browser Company and an engineering leader at Slack and Meta. The two have built together since 2011, from Google to Foursquare to Slack. Scuba is the duo’s fourth tour together.
How Scuba works for teams:
Never lose a great idea. Capture articles, screenshots, files, videos, and threads from your browser or apps. Get instant summaries and highlights.
Scale your team’s best thinking. Turn individual expertise into a shared advantage. Collections keep everyone aligned on launches, key clients, company strategy, and competitive shifts, with Scuba automatically organizing every shared Capture.
Stay aligned and ahead. Scuba connects the dots across your team’s thinking, surfacing emerging trends, important changes, and potential conflicts through daily Briefings or on-demand Sessions.
Never start from scratch again. Get feedback, pressure-test ideas, and create proposals grounded in your team’s Captures. Always with citations, and fresh web sources when needed.
Get more leverage from your agents. Connect Scuba to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and more through MCP, or bring @Scuba into Slack. Every answer, document, and line of code starts with your team’s unique context.
Capture and catch up on the go. Save ideas, links, screenshots, and voice notes with full transcripts wherever you are, with seamless syncing across devices.
“The frontier models aren't intelligence bound. They're context constrained,” said Noah Desai Weiss, co-founder and CEO of Scuba. “That’s why we're building Scuba. So people never lose a great idea again. For companies that want to move smarter together. For teams with a mind of their own. We aim to be the 1% of AI spend that makes the other 99% pay off.”
"Breakthrough products have the power to change how teams work together. Slack did it for team communication with channels. Cursor did it for writing code with AI. Now Scuba is doing it for team alignment with shared context," said Andrew Braccia, Partner at Accel. "Noah and Dolapo have spent nearly two decades building beloved products at large scale. As the pace of work keeps speeding up, the team at Scuba is building something that will help every team scale their own taste and expertise to go faster together."
"Without understanding a team's shared judgment, agents can never achieve their full potential. Noah and Dolapo spent their careers getting the right information to the right people at the right moment, which is why we knew they were the right founders to solve this problem," said Shravan Narayen, General Partner at IVP.
For the past six months, hundreds of early users have run on Scuba in private beta. They’ve used it to build products, run launches, track customer feedback, develop company strategy, and explore new markets. The prevailing sentiment from early adopters: “Scuba helps me feel like a smarter version of myself because what I learn compounds.”
The new funding will accelerate product expansion, hiring, and go-to-market. Scuba is opening the limited beta to teams in waves. Teams can apply for early access at scuba.app .
ABOUT SCUBA
Scuba is the shared context engine for teams and their agents. It's the shared memory teams have been missing, keeping teams and their agents continuously aligned. Founded by former Slack leaders Noah Desai Weiss and Dolapo Falola, Scuba is based in New York and backed by Accel, IVP, BoxGroup, Conviction, Homebrew, and Scribble Ventures.
Learn more: scuba.app
Follow Scuba: X | LinkedIn | Instagram | YouTube

Duvo Raises $32 Million Series A to Become the One Platform Enterprises Run Their Operations On
October 14, 2026
Duvo
Duvo Raises $32 Million Series A to Become the One Platform Enterprises Run Their Operations On
PR Newswire
NEW YORK and LONDON, Oct. 14, 2026
Led by Balderton Capital, the round funds Duvo’s U.S. expansion. Its Enterprise Execution OS lets people and AI agents run processes together across the systems a company already has, starting with retail and consumer goods.
NEW YORK and LONDON , Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Duvo today announced a $32 million Series A led by Balderton Capital, with participation from existing investors Index Ventures, Northzone and Credo Ventures. The round brings Duvo’s total funding to $48 million and will fund its expansion, starting with retailers and CPG companies. Two executives lead the expansion. Michael Green joins from Databricks as Chief Commercial Officer. He previously served as a Senior Vice President at Salesforce. Spencer Insolia recently joined as Managing Director, U.S. He was previously President of Kmart and a Managing Director at Accenture.
Duvo is the Enterprise Execution OS: one platform where a company’s operations run, with governed processes and clear user approvals. Duvo is built so that AI in operations doesn’t stop at the pilot. Every process a company adds runs on the same connections, the same approval rules and the same record of results, instead of becoming another standalone project.
The platform works the same way for every process. Duvo Clarity captures how the work really runs, through AI-led discovery interviews with the people who do it, screen recordings and existing documents. Duvo’s agents then run the approved steps across ERPs, supplier portals, spreadsheets and inboxes, through APIs where they exist and through the same screens people use where they don’t. That’s why Duvo can be live in weeks with the first process without a small army of engineers or a major systems integration project.
Decisions and exceptions go to the person who owns them, and operating cockpits show what is waiting for a decision and what the process delivered. Most companies run on systems that don’t talk to each other, and the manual work in those gaps is where value leaks. Duvo runs that work on one platform and recovers the value.
Gartner projects spending on business orchestration and automation technologies will exceed $21 billion by 2029, as enterprises consolidate fragmented automation tools onto a single platform. But turning that into operational results is proving hard. Gartner predicts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. In a separate survey of 350 executives at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue, Gartner found that those reporting higher returns from AI agents and automation had cut staff about as often as those with modest or negative results.
“For a while I measured AI in heads, counting how many people an agent could replace. It’s the wrong unit,” said Tomáš Čupr, co-founder and CEO of Duvo and founder and Group CEO of Rohlik Group. “At Rohlik, the gains I’d point to came from work nobody had the hours for. Our planners used to check about eight at-risk products a day per market for shortages. Now every signal gets checked, around the clock. We think of it as raising the GDP of every employee: more value from the people a company has, not the same value from fewer of them.”
Duvo has unlocked over $100m+ for its clients, across finance, supply chain, commercial, customer care, marketing and HR. At Notino, Europe’s largest online beauty retailer, those results span finance, customer care and marketing. Its quarterly reconciliation of about $45 million a year in supplier bonuses went from 70 days to 15, and from around 120 specialist hours per cycle to under 10.
“Our business processes have evolved over decades, and Duvo gives us a way to understand them in detail, and quickly,” said Gordon MacPherson, Group Productivity Director at U.K. supermarket chain Morrisons. “It means decisions about which repetitive everyday tasks to simplify, redesign and automate can be based on evidence rather than assumptions. That gives us a much clearer path from identifying AI opportunities to putting them into operation, freeing up our people to concentrate on high-value work for the benefit of colleagues and customers.”
“Getting AI agents to work reliably across the enterprise remains incredibly difficult,” said Rob Moffat, Partner at Balderton Capital. “Duvo’s unique ability is in how it uses AI to capture how work actually happens in the enterprise and what the causes of loss are. Duvo then automates these processes in the same integrated system. This is only possible with the deep operational experience of the founder Tomáš who previously founded three companies including Rohlik, the leading online grocer. Feedback from customers and consultancy partners is off the charts positive. We are looking forward to supporting Tomáš and team as they build the global leader in this segment.”
Duvo is model-agnostic, so the AI underneath can change without rebuilding the processes on top of it. Companies with stricter security or sovereignty requirements can run open-weight models on dedicated GPUs, connect a model in their own cloud or on-premises, or use an AI endpoint they already approve. Every approval and every change written back to a company’s systems is recorded. Duvo is SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 certified, and U.S. companies can buy it through Microsoft’s Azure Marketplace.
“Our clients don’t need more AI pilots. Startup Spotlight
Optivolt Raises $32M Series A to Build the Brain for Solar Panels
October 21, 2026
Optivolt (Techstars 2018) has raised a $32M Series A to scale its Power Balancer, technology built into the solar panel that recovers energy lost to shade, dirt, and wear in real time. The funding will expand manufacturing and bring Optivolt to residential, commercial, and utility-scale projects, including ones that power AI data centers.
Optivolt (Techstars 2018) has raised a $32M Series A, bringing the company's total funding to $42M.
Optivolt builds power electronics that live inside the solar panel itself. Its core technology, the Power Balancer, helps panels produce more energy in the messy conditions they face every day, from shade and dirt to weather and uneven wear over time. The new funding will expand manufacturing and bring the technology to residential, commercial, and utility-scale projects, including installations built to power AI data centers.
Momentum Behind the Round
More than 20,000 solar panels with the Power Balancer have already shipped. Optivolt holds 19 issued patents with 27 more pending, and has earned UL certifications covering its junction box enclosure, panel-integrated electronics, rapid-shutdown system, and module safety.
The Problem With Today's Solar Panels
Solar has become one of the cheapest sources of new power. Still, a typical panel loses a meaningful share of its output whenever part of it is shaded, dirty, or wearing unevenly. Conventional panels rely on bypass diodes to route around underperforming cells, which protects the panel but leaves energy on the table. Many installers add separate optimizers or microinverters to recover some of that loss, adding hardware and cost to every system.
How the Power Balancer Works
The Power Balancer redistributes energy among groups of cells within a panel in real time. When one section is struggling, the system rebalances so the rest of the panel keeps producing. It replaces conventional bypass diodes and builds rapid shutdown and monitoring directly into the panel. Depending on the system design, that can reduce or remove the need for separate optimizers, microinverters, and rapid-shutdown devices.
Optivolt reports that the Power Balancer runs at 99.4% conversion efficiency under typical operating conditions. In the company's internal testing under defined shading scenarios, panels with its technology produced up to six times the power of panels using bolted-on optimizers.
What's Next
With the Series A closed, Optivolt will scale up production and speed deployment across residential, commercial, and utility-scale solar. Data centers are a growing focus, as demand for power from AI workloads continues to climb.
The People Building It
Optivolt was founded by Rohit Kalyanpur, a Thiel Fellow who has spent nine years rebuilding the solar panel from first principles.
"Solar became cheap enough to compete. I founded Optivolt to make it intelligent enough to power the world," said Rohit Kalyanpur, founder and CEO of Optivolt. "The result is the first solar panel system that thinks for itself... The next step is putting it everywhere."
To learn more, visit optivolt.com .

The best artificial intelligence model in the world scores 51% on a realistic private-equity due-diligence simulation — and a nine-person San Francisco company just raised $30 million Series A to sell the labs responsible for those models the training infrastructure they need to improve.
Halluminate, founded in 2024 by CEO Jerry Wu and CTO Wyatt Marshall, announced a Series A led by Oak HC/FT on October 1, 2026, bringing the company's total funding to $38.5 million. Existing investors Y Combinator, Orange Collective, Heavybit, and FT Partners participated in the round, as did individual researchers from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta as angels — a customer list that doubles as a cap table.
What Finance Due Diligence Reveals About AI's Real Ceiling
In August, Halluminate published a benchmark it calls the Westworld Finance Diligence Bench — 88 tasks drawn from anonymized real private-equity transactions, written and reviewed by practicing deal professionals. Seven frontier models ran through it. The highest average score, across all seven models , was 51%.
That ceiling is worth examining closely. Halluminate designed the benchmark to simulate the complete body of work that a team of investment bankers, consultants, and accountants would produce together over several weeks: document review, contract analysis, evolving term sheets, and final deliverables. One benchmark task required an agent to redline a statement of work while navigating a 160-file data room, 21 emails across nine threads, and four sets of meeting notes — with deal terms changing throughout and certain provisions meant to remain fixed regardless.
Across the benchmark, agents consistently failed in the same ways: leaving out required changes, applying the wrong analytical method, or acting on information that had already been superseded. The failure wasn't in any single step. It was in carrying instructions through to the end — maintaining context and intent across a long, messy, real-world workflow.
These failure patterns are Halluminate's raw material. The company turns each identified breakdown into a reinforcement-learning environment: a structured, interactive simulation where a model can attempt the failing task, receive feedback, and iterate — without touching a real deal or a real data room.
Why Financial Work Is Harder to Simulate Than Code
The technical obstacle that makes finance-specific RL environments both more difficult to build and more valuable than their coding-domain equivalents comes down to a single engineering requirement: the reward function must be verifiable without a human reviewing every output.
Coding environments solve this cleanly. Run the code, check whether the tests pass. The outcome is binary and programmable. The reason OpenAI's reasoning models and Anthropic's Claude family improved so rapidly on coding benchmarks is that coding offers unlimited programmatic verifiability at the scale RL training requires — which can mean millions of individual task attempts per training run, according to Scale AI's analysis .
Financial work does not offer that. Whether a contract clause is correctly redlined depends on the current deal terms, the provisions meant to survive, the legal precedent governing that type of clause, and what a senior banker would consider acceptable versus unacceptable. A program cannot check that. Only an expert rubric can — and building expert rubrics requires practitioners who have done the work.
Halluminate's approach to this problem is to source its benchmark tasks from anonymized actual transactions reviewed by active deal professionals. The expert rubric is the verifier, built into the environment itself. Wu describes the systems the company builds as infrastructure for "verticalized data research labs" — compounding financial expertise and professional judgment into a training signal, rather than spreading thin across many industries.
Why Frontier Lab Customers Pay for This
According to Wu, four of the five leading closed-source US AI labs are paying customers of Halluminate. The company has crossed what it describes as a mid-eight-figure annualized revenue run rate — a figure Wu characterizes as based on quarterly revenue already delivered and paid for — and is profitable.
That profitability at nine employees reflects a concentrated, high-value customer base that has no obvious substitute. Frontier labs have invested heavily in coding RL environments — the highest-demand category in the post-training infrastructure market, according to reporting from SemiAnalysis and others — but financial work has not received the same attention. The labs doing the most capable general AI research are not financial services firms. They have the engineering talent to build general environments but not the professional network, deal-flow access, or practitioner relationships to build finance-specific ones. Halluminate has both.
Oak HC/FT General Partner Matt Streisfeld, whose firm led the round, explained the investment rationale directly: finance offers an unusually broad and complex range of knowledge work, spanning banking, private equity, consulting, and accounting. As AI agents move from tasks that take seconds to tasks that stretch over hours and days, he expects the quality of the training environment to become decisive.
"When the agent starts getting into long horizon work," Streisfeld told Fortune, "testing work and specialization will really be key."
What Makes Finance AI a Hot Market Right Now

candidates.title: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
candidates.snippet: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Tolan , the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital.
The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media . (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”)
Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos.
Image Credits: Tolan on App Store
Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.”
The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular to neurodivergent people , who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.)
Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “ very cringe ,” The New York Times called it “hated,” and Wired said it “has no soul.”
Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently filed for bankruptcy after its founder’s return to Google . (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.)
However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to release as a hardware product in the future.
The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that multiple lawsuits have been filed against general-purpose AI app makers alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides.

RapidCanvas Raises $29M Series B to Bring Fortune 100-Grade AI to Every Enterprise
Led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India with participation from Hitachi Ventures, the round will scale RapidCanvas’ Hybrid Approach™, pairing its AI platform with field AI engineers.
AUSTIN, Texas, Oct. 16, 2026 - RapidCanvas , the managed AI execution company pioneering the Hybrid Approach to deliver custom AI solutions at SaaS economics, has raised $29 million in Series B funding led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India with participation from Hitachi Ventures. Existing investors Accel, Peak XV Partners, Valley Capital Partners and Titanium Ventures also participated in the round. The financing brings total funding to $52.5 million. The raise follows 8x growth in annual recurring revenue over the past six quarters as enterprises demand outcomes from custom AI in production. More than 40% of RapidCanvas’ customers now run multiple AI use cases in production.
RapidCanvas pairs its AI platform with field AI engineers to deliver custom AI solutions. AI engineers learn each customer’s business processes, design and build custom AI applications, and stay accountable for the applications’ outcomes after delivery. The RapidCanvas AI platform brings together three products: The Enterprise Context Engine™ lets an enterprise capture how a business process runs, from requirements and tribal knowledge to data schemas and decision history, and the enterprise owns that context. The Visual Development Canvas lets AI engineers rapidly build custom AI solutions that meet industry benchmarks, drawing on a skills library that gives each new solution a 60% head start from proven, benchmarked code. The Operational Harness manages and governs AI solutions once they’re deployed in production. RapidCanvas offers its Hybrid Approach at subscription pricing, changing the economics of enterprise AI.
So far in 2026, more than 75 enterprises in manufacturing, financial services, retail, business services and infrastructure have made 1.4 million AI-led decisions with applications built on RapidCanvas.
“AI can be the great equalizer, but so far its biggest wins have gone to the Fortune 100. We want to give every enterprise the same opportunity,” said Rahul Pangam, co-founder and CEO of RapidCanvas . “Vibe coding has made it easy to start building with AI. Getting AI into production reliably and safely still remains the biggest gap. Our growth over the past six quarters is evidence that AI in enterprises is moving beyond pilots into production and real operations.”
RapidCanvas serves an underserved market: enterprises with $100 million to $10 billion in revenue that have AI budgets and C-suite mandates but no proven path to outcomes. These companies are caught between services firms that charge millions and take months to deliver, and do-it-yourself platforms that require specialized AI talent most of them don’t have. In conversations with more than 400 business leaders, RapidCanvas found that most C-level executives expect a return on AI within six to 12 months, yet very few have moved beyond pilots and proofs of concept.
“Most enterprises are still searching for real returns on their AI spend. RapidCanvas delivers them by pairing an AI platform that compounds with every deployment and field AI engineers who own the outcome end to end. The proof is in the customer pull: enterprises keep expanding into new use cases and functions. We’re excited to lead this Series B and back a team that has built and scaled this playbook before.” said Piyush Kharbanda, General Partner at Vertex Ventures SEA & India .
“Enterprise AI will ultimately be measured by the economics of delivering outcomes at scale. RapidCanvas combines hands-on engineering with a productized platform, allowing what starts as custom delivery to become increasingly repeatable and scalable. That shift from services economics toward software economics is core to our AInomics thesis at Hitachi Ventures, and we’re glad to partner with the team as they scale,” said Radhika Ananth, Head of India and Investment Director at Hitachi Ventures .
RapidCanvas will use the Series B funding to grow its go-to-market teams and expand its network of private equity and advisory partners, who bring managed AI execution to their portfolio companies and clients as a repeatable path to value. It will also grow its field AI engineering team across the U.S., Brazil and India. The company will invest in all three of its products: deepening the Enterprise Context Engine, growing the skills library behind the Visual Development Canvas, and strengthening governance in the Operational Harness.
About RapidCanvas
RapidCanvas is a managed AI execution company that takes organizations from concept to production to scaled transformation. The RapidCanvas Hybrid Approach™ pairs elite human experts with a purpose-built agentic platform, delivering solutions that are human-led, agent-executed, and outcome-first. Partners include leaders in manufacturing, retail/consumer goods, financial services, business services, supply chain, and infrastructure. Recognized as a top 5 Data Science and Machine Learning platform by G2. See rapidcanvas.ai .
About Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India
Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India is a leading early-stage venture capital firm focused on partnering with high-growth startups across Southeast Asia and India. With a strong network and strategic expertise, they have invested in successful companies such as Grab, FirstCry, Nium, Licious, Kuku FM, Abacus Digital, RPG Commerce and PatSnap, driving innovation and scaling businesses across various sectors. See - https://www.vertexventures.sg

Exclusive: Slingshot Raises $27M In Seed Funding To Build An Insurer For Those Small Policies Sold At Checkout
Exclusive: Slingshot Raises $27M In Seed Funding To Build An Insurer For Those Small Policies Sold At Checkout
22 Oct, 2026 by Crunchbase
Join Our Socials
Share
Slingshot Insurance, an AI-native embedded insurance startup, is emerging from stealth with $27 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively.
Rally Ventures and Skyward Group co-led the round, with participation from insurance industry veterans including Jim Hays , who will join Slingshot’s board. Rally is also a co-founder of the Minneapolis-based startup, as part of the firm’s broader approach. So far, it has co-founded roughly eight portfolio companies that have either launched or remain in stealth.
Ethan Genteman, co-founder and CEO of Slingshot Insurance. (Courtesy photo)
Slingshot, which is led by first-time founder and CEO Ethan Genteman, focuses on small insurance policies that consumers can buy as part of another purchase, such as coverage when booking a flight. Known as embedded insurance, the model puts coverage in front of customers when they might need it.
The startup’s software helps businesses offer those policies by connecting them with insurers that back the coverage. It uses AI to process and share data between the two sides, aiming to reduce the administrative work that can make inexpensive policies costly to offer.
Its first customer and design partner is Vertical Insure , which serves more than 750,000 customers at an average premium of $25, according to Slingshot. Genteman told Crunchbase News that Slingshot’s first program will launch this month.
For now, Slingshot earns revenue as a technology provider working with outside insurers. But the six-person company, which formally began operating July 1, is also pursuing an acquisition that would allow it to back policies itself.
“We’re not a carrier yet, but we are rapidly closing on our carrier,” Genteman said in an interview.
Making the math work on a $25 policy
One product Slingshot is working on would let parents buy insurance when signing a child up for youth sports, Genteman said. A parent spending $2,000 on a volleyball league, for example, might be offered a $25 policy covering cancellation or an injury during the season.
Each policy includes paperwork and coordination with an insurer, and can bring potential claims. But when policies cost so little, managing them can quickly eat into the money they bring in, noted Genteman.
He believes that as vertical SaaS companies increasingly look beyond traditional subscription fees for growth, embedded insurance is “a largely untapped opportunity” to generate incremental revenue from transactions already happening on their platforms while delivering additional value to customers.
“The challenge is that the insurance and regulatory landscape is incredibly complex, and most SaaS companies don’t have the expertise, industry relationships or understanding of where to begin,” he said.
Slingshot aims to solve this by providing a white-glove service for those vertical SaaS companies, helping them go from an insurance product idea to “a fully operational offering.”
He offered a hypothetical example: A program collecting $500,000 in premiums with a 10% margin would have just $50,000 in margin.
“That’s not a viable program for the way incumbent carriers have set themselves up operationally,” he said.
Slingshot’s goal is to replace the spreadsheets, emails and disconnected systems used to manage that work with software that connects policy distributors and insurers directly. The company says its AI automates data-heavy tasks while keeping a record of decisions that the businesses involved can review and check.
It charges a 5% technology fee to administer programs through its platform. Acquiring an insurer would let it provide both the software and the financial backing, according to Genteman.
A customer helped shape the business
The difficulties facing Slingshot’s first customer helped bring the startup together.
Rally had already helped start Vertical Insure, which uses software platforms to sell insurance to its customers. According to Genteman, that business had opportunities to introduce more products but struggled to find insurers whose technology and processes could keep up.
“We can design the products our customers need almost overnight, but the industry is highly regulated, and we need delegated authority just to write and distribute what we’ve built,” Vertical Insure co-founder and CEO Brock Noland said in a statement. “The antiquated approval process on the carrier-side slows everything down.”
Even after finding an insurer willing to back a product, connecting the two companies’ systems could create more delays, Genteman said.
Slingshot was built to address those problems, with Vertical Insure helping shape its product as a design partner. Noland is also a Slingshot co-founder.
The opportunity in vertical SaaS
Genteman sees a broader opening among vertical SaaS companies: businesses that sell software tailored to a particular industry.
As vertical SaaS companies look for ways to grow beyond subscription fees, insurance could give them another avenue to make money from purchases customers already make through their platforms, argues Genteman. They already know their customers and what they’re buying, putting them in a position to offer coverage that fits the purchase.
A babysitting platform, for example, could offer coverage to help parents pay for replacement childcare if a sitter cancels at the last minute. Software used by pet boarding facilities could offer coverage for unexpected vet bills if a pet is injured during a stay. An equipment rental platform could let customers add protection at checkout against accidental damage or theft.

candidates.title: WhiteLab Genomics raises $26M Series B to design genomic medicines with AI
candidates.snippet: WhiteLab Genomics raises $26M Series B to design genomic medicines with AI Dealroom
candidates.text:
Fundraise Oct 5, 2026, 21:28 UTC
WhiteLab Genomics raises $26M Series B to design genomic medicines with AI
What's the deal? WhiteLab Genomics , a genomic medicine developer, has raised a $26 million Series B led by AVP Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , chief executive officer David Del Bourgo told Axios Pro. Omnes Capital Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , Yaday Health, Blast Club Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , and Debiopharm Innovation Fund Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → joined the round, which brings total funding to about $37 million.
How it works: WhiteLab's Alfred platform uses AI to design viral and non-viral delivery vehicles and programmable genetic payloads. The designs are then experimentally validated and tested in vivo to identify drug candidates. The company says the process cuts the time and cost of developing genomic medicines.
What's the endgame? Rather than taking assets to the clinic itself, WhiteLab runs about 15 revenue-generating partnerships with biotechs and large pharmaceutical firms, including Sanofi . Other partners include Cytiva Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , Debiopharm Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , the University of Massachusetts Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , the Vision Institute Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → in Paris, and the Paris Brain Institute Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → .
"We specialize in what we're very good at doing … bringing preclinical assets to their highest level of validation as possible, and then partnering with pharma," Del Bourgo said.
Why now? The funding arrives as the life sciences sector recovers from a multiyear slump. Biopharma venture funding topped $10 billion in Q2 — only the third quarter above that mark since early 2022, per PitchBook.
Behind the scenes: Del Bourgo said he is open to being acquired and that buyers have approached WhiteLab, though it would also consider a US IPO. The company has two to three years of runway.
AVP managing partner François Robinet framed the appeal of the model: "You have the best of both worlds because you are paid for providing the platform, and you are paid in case of success (in) the drug development process."
The signal: At $26 million, the round sits in the upper third of comparable deals by size — a sign that investors are again backing platform plays that generate revenue through partnerships rather than betting on a single clinical asset.

candidates.title: Nirva Raises $25M Pre-Series A for an AI Pendant That Listens only to its Wearer
candidates.snippet: Nirva Raises $25M Pre-Series A for an AI Pendant That Listens only to its Wearer AI Funding Tracker
candidates.text:
Ambient AI is having a moment. Amazon launched a new wrist-worn device with Bee; a former Plaud exec launched ambient apps through a startup called Ambi, which aims to also build its own hardware; and Apple launched Voice Intelligence features during its iPhone launch in September. Now, a company called Nirva is betting on a jewelry-like pendant and its ability to listen only to the wearer.
The startup today announced a new $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to the $8 million it raised earlier in the year from investors like Lightspeed and South Park Commons, bringing its total raise to $33 million.
Nirva was founded in 2025 by two former Meta Reality Labs employees, Wei Lyu and Jason Chen, along with Hanying Hu, who founded a fashion and jewelry brand.
The company’s first device is a pendant, which can also be worn as a bracelet. The device weighs only around eight grams, making it easy to wear all day. Its battery lasts up to three days on a single charge.
Longer term, Nirva aims to release more devices.
Image Credits: Nirva
In a call with TechCrunch, Nirva CEO Lyu said that the company wanted to build a wearable that blends in with fashion, but also provides value to users.
“This is a piece of jewelry that only focuses on listening to your own speech. We are not like a voice recorder or like a meeting note taker. One key difference between us, Taya, Vocci, or Sandbar Ring is that we’re always passively listening to your own speech. So it’s always on. It keeps modeling the user and modeling your mind,” Lyu said.
For ambient devices, privacy is a big question, as people might not like to be recorded all the time. Plus, devices like the Ray-Ban Meta have instilled fear in those who are around the person wearing the smart glasses that they are being recorded too.
Nirva gets around this problem by asking users to record snippets of their voice during onboarding and building its model based on that. During use, the device filters out conversations or data captured from the other people around the device. That means it’s only recording the wearer.
In addition, Nirva by default doesn’t keep any audio data or transcripts after processing the conversations.
Nirva is positioning itself as a personal insights company rather than a productivity startup. However, its app shows you reminders or action items and ways to act on them. Lyu said that through its app, the startup wants to help users show up for others in a better way in their lives.
“I think there’s no universal way to help everyone to solve their problems. We are building a tool to help people to improve their self-understanding, self-compassion, and self-awareness,” Lyu said.
Image Credits: Nirva
The companion app parses users’ speech and creates insights that it infers are related to the user’s personality, including patterns, the people who tend to be around them, the places they’ve been to, and other daily notes. Lyu emphasized that the app shows users insights around their emotions, communication style, and ways they can improve.
Lyu gave an example of an incident when she forgot to thank her mother for something, and the app later nudged her with a reminder about this.
The company also said that, before it discards the audio, it’s able to track the tone, pitch, volume, and speed, which are useful for deriving emotion-related understandings that are then surfaced in the app.
Nirva will start taking orders for its devices in November, with an aim to ship them to early users by the end of the year. The $249 device will be available in silver, brushed silver, black, and gold.
The startup has competition in the AI wearables area. There are companies like former Apple employees’ Taya , which is also building intelligent jewelry. Plus, startups like Friend and Bee are trying to be companion gadgets as well.

candidates.snippet: Ex-Ramp engineers raise $20M for platform Melius after scrapping their first product TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Featured
Ex-Ramp engineers raise $20M for platform Melius after scrapping their first product
Melius, an AI platform for ad campaign generation, has raised $25 million in funding. The startup, founded by ex-Ramp engineers, pivoted from its initial product to focus on creative asset generation.
By Marina Temkin · Oct 6 · techcrunch.com · 2 min read
Intelligence analysis by Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite
Image: techcrunch.com
Founded by former Ramp engineers, Melius has secured $25 million in funding to develop its AI platform for generating ad campaigns, images, and videos. The company pivoted significantly after its initial product failed to gain traction, scrapping its codebase to focus on creative asset generation, a move that has already yielded over $1 million in annualized revenue.
Why it matters
This story highlights the resilience of founders in the startup ecosystem, demonstrating how a significant pivot after initial product failure can lead to substantial funding and early revenue traction, offering a case study for other early-stage companies.
Explain like I'm 10 years old
Imagine you want to make cool ads for toys, but drawing and filming is hard. Melius is like a super-smart robot helper that can create the pictures and videos for your ads just by you telling it what you want, using simple words. It got a lot of money to build this helper, even after its first try didn't work out.
Analysis
Melius
Melius, an AI platform focused on generating creative assets for advertising, has successfully raised $25 million in funding, comprising a $20 million Series A led by CRV and a $5 million seed round from General Catalyst. This significant capital infusion comes after the company, founded by former engineers from the corporate spending software company Ramp, made a decisive pivot. Initially, Melius aimed to build an AI-powered performance marketing tool to help marketers manage and optimize ad spend. However, after investing over six months into development, the co-founders realized the original concept lacked viability.
Scrapping the Codebase
Co-founder Joowon Kim candidly admitted that the team "scrapped the entire codebase" and "burned all of it" to pursue a new direction. This drastic measure was taken because the initial AI-powered performance marketing tool "didn’t have legs." Instead of optimizing ad spend, the team identified a larger opportunity in creating the tools that generate the actual creative content for ad campaigns. This strategic shift led to the development of a new platform, described as an "agents lab for creative work," which has already achieved over $1 million in annualized revenue within two months of launching in July.
Market Landscape
The AI-powered creative asset generation space is becoming increasingly crowded, with notable competitors like Higgsfield, which recently achieved a $5.4 billion valuation. Other emerging players include Krea and Flora AI. Despite the competitive landscape, Kim expressed confidence, citing the vast size of the market as sufficient to support multiple companies. He views the presence of numerous competitors as an indicator of strong demand and ample opportunities for new entrants to capture market share and win customers. Kim's personal passion for digital media creation, stemming from childhood aspirations of becoming a YouTuber, fuels his drive to build tools that democratize content creation.
Key points
Melius, founded by ex-Ramp engineers, raised $25 million in funding.
The company pivoted from an ad spend optimization tool to an AI creative asset generator.
Melius achieved over $1 million in annualized revenue within two months of its new product launch.
The founders scrapped their initial codebase to pursue the new product direction.
Despite a competitive market, Melius believes the demand is large enough for multiple players.
The Upside
The company's successful pivot and rapid revenue generation suggest strong market demand for AI-driven creative tools. With substantial funding, Melius is well-positioned to scale its platform and capture significant market share in the burgeoning AI advertising space.
The Downside
The AI creative generation market is highly competitive, with well-funded players like Higgsfield. Melius faces the challenge of differentiating its platform and maintaining its rapid growth trajectory amidst intense competition and evolving AI technology.
Originally reported at techcrunch.com
Discernion covers the story. Read the full piece at the source.
